tickets.question: Hello, my friend needs to figure out how her job was classified under civil service laws. Do you know what the term "TEMPORARY OJ", as found in the NYC Civil Service Titles, means? If a legend explains that, I haven't found it. My best guess is "Temporary Office Job". I would also like to know if that designation is within the labor, exempt, competitive, or noncompetitive class, or if it has not yet been assigned within those classified classes. Thank you for your time!
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting NYC Open Data Help Desk. A title marked “OJ” refers to “Original Jurisdiction”, which indicates that the title is not represented by a union and has salary ranges set by the Mayor pursuant to the Mayor’s authority under the City Charter.
A temporary title is one that has been proposed and is pending the completion of the formal classification process.
A temporary OJ title could be proposed for either the Non-Competitive or Exempt Class.
​
Thank you,
-NYC Open Data

tickets.question: How can i reduce the number of columns before downloading the data. I just want 20 columns of the 41 available in the 311 SR calls data set.
tickets.reply:
​Thank you for contacting NYC Open Data Help Desk. There are 2 ways in which you can delimit the number of columns you would like to export.
​
​1. If you have an account with Socrata and you logged in, you can create a derived view from a dataset or filtered view, save that derived view, and then hide columns through the column editor modal in grid view. After saving those changes in the view, the remaining data can be exported using the Export option in grid view. To signup for the account, please visit this URL: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/signup
​
​2. Without needing to create a derived view, a user can write a SoQL query from the SODA API endoint using a "Select" parameter to explicitly specify the desired columns. Please note that API defaults the limit to 1000, so you will need to set the limit to accommodate 311 dataset. After viewing the .json to verify that they you are getting the expected results from their query, you can change the end of the URL from .json to .csv in order to download those results as a CSV.
​
​For questions regarding API and other technical issue, please direct inquires to Socrata support at https://support.socrata.com/hc/en-us

Thank you,
- NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question:
Dear whom it may concern,

Starting in July of 2019, there was a 20% drop vs. the proceeding four years (i.e., 2015-2018) in the number of calls going to 311, as evidenced by the NYC “311 Service Requests from 2010 to Present” data. Was this related to changes in the 311 system? We know that sometime in the last two years, the city began transitioning to a new IBM Watson-based system. We would like to know any dates or milestones from the switchover that might have materially impacted 311 data. If this drop has nothing to do with the change in 311 system, we would like to know whether there was another cause we should know about.

Best Regards,
https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Social-Services/311-Service-Requests-from-2010-to-Present/erm2-nwe9
tickets.reply:
Hi,

Thank you for your patience as we work to contact the appropriate agency in teams.

In 2010, HRA had a special Advantage subsidy hotline that was answered by 311. The call takers answered what they could and then created service tickets for staff at DHS to answer. The service tickets were split into landlord, tenant, and advocate calls for tracking purposes. Landlords called about payment and tenant issues, tenants called about annual renewals, apartment conditions, and service requests, and third parties like brokers or case managers called on behalf of the landlords and tenants for similar issues.

Thank you,
- NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question:
For the 311 data, the portal says: "NOTE: This data does not present a full picture of 311 calls or service requests, in part because of operational and system complexities associated with remote call taking necessitated by the unprecedented volume 311 is handling during the Covid-19 crisis. The City is working to address this issue."

If you have the info, can you say a little bit about how the data is not representative? Any sense of the scale of incompleteness? And is there any update on what's being done to address the issue (totally recognizing the amazing hard work that goes into making this available in the first place!)?

Many thanks for all your work.

Are the lat/lon coordinates that of the caller or that of the location of the issue?
Thank you!
tickets.reply:
The incident address is identified by the customer and geo-validated by our system. The incident address is the location of the incident as reported by the customer. There is no relationship to where the customer is located at the time of the report, except in the case of mobile app SRs - the app will show the users location on a map if the user has location services enabled. The user in that case would have to confirm the location as the incident location. You can see the source channel in the ‘Open Data Channel Type’ column.

Thank you,
- NYC 311 Open Data

tickets.question: I'm using the 311 data (filtered between 2016-11 to 2021-10, complaint type = Dirty Condition, Dirty Conditions) to work on my waste management project. I realized that some of the data was missing for 2021-10 and the number of calls is significantly lower. 2021-10 is also when DSNY stopped updating sidewalk rating data. Was there any organizational change that caused this? Please let me know if the agency is using another name for the complaint type or datasets.
tickets.reply:
There are multiple reasons for the issues that you noticed. Due to the rollout of a new system to handle 311 service requests in September 2021, a number of old complaint types were deprecated and merged with new complaint types. For example, “Dirty Conditions” that existed before is now only known as “Dirty Condition”. The descriptors associated with complaints have also been deprecated, and some don’t exist anymore.

The Department of Sanitation is currently working with DoITT (the Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications) to figure out a technical solution to connect the old and new complaint types so that historical comparisons can be made. Once the data is corrected by DoITT, the 311 datasets will have to be republished. We cannot provide a timeframe when this will happen since we do not control this process.

Please note that the Scorecard Inspection program, which measures and reports on street and sidewalk cleanliness across the city’s five boroughs, is a program managed through the Mayor’s Office of Operations (not the Department of Sanitation) so you will need to direct your questions regarding this program to them. Here is a link to the webpage that contains the latest Scorecard Inspection reports: https://www1.nyc.gov/site/operations/performance/scorecard-street-sidewalk-cleanliness-ratings.page.

I hope you find this information helpful.

Thank you,
- NYC DSNY Open Data

Hope this helps!

Thank you,
NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question: Under the problem detail field, what does it mean when the field say "Snow Tracking"?
tickets.reply: Snow Tracking is used to identify Rapid Snow SRs that are automatically closed upon creation during active snow and ice events. These SRs support situational awareness by tracking snow and icy conditions reported through snow complaint routes across the city.

tickets.question: Hello, I am researching how public datasets can be used to understand community needs and access to services in large cities. I would like to know whether this dataset includes any fields that can help identify trends related to mental health, social support, or public well-being requests over time. Are there any recommended fields, filters, or related datasets that would be useful for this type of research?
tickets.reply:
We recommend starting with the dataset's data dictionary, available on the dataset page under "Attachments." It is also linked here for your convenience (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/views/erm2-nwe9/files/c5cc6926-45bb-4af3-8aab-0ee6a29bcf4d?download=true&filename=311_ServiceRequest_2020-present_DataDictionary_Updated_2025.xlsx)
The dictionary includes a tab called "All Agencies Complaint<>Details" that maps every agency to its complaint types and descriptors. You can use it to identify which complaint categories are relevant to your research themes before filtering the dataset itself.
If you have further questions for the 311 Team, feel free to write back.

tickets.question: Not a question, but a suggestion. It's cool that they decided to include community boards as a geographic identifier! I would also suggest adding a column that says what neighborhoods these community boards serve. For example, all 01 Bronx CBs would say "Melrose, Mott Haven, Port Morris"

This dataset is huge and updates frequently and the field mutates with not indicator of which row was updated (or when a particular row was updated), this means anyone trying to make use of the data will need to re-download the whole set everytime, which is time consuming and a waste of bandwidth. 
I'd like to request adding a column that shows timestamp of revision when the row was changed so that downstream processing can be streamlined and the row can be used to filter to reduce wasted bandwidth
tickets.reply: Hi, thank you for your question! It sounds like you may want to access new data using an API. This would let you select newly updated rows without having to manually filter or download them. Within the API there is a "created_at" field which shows when it was last updated. If you need any assistance using APIs our vendor has provided some guides:  https://dev.socrata.com/consumers/getting-started.html

tickets.reply:
There was no redistricting of the election districts between 2014 and 2018 so they will be virtually identical. Generally, the election districts would only change after a Census update (2-3 years after, i.e. 2010 Census -> redistrict in 2012 or 2013).

The election districts are aligned with the City Street Centerline dataset so if there was a slight adjustment to the street centerline, the election district boundaries would reflect that adjustment.

We also make archived versions of the all of our district boundary files available here:
https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/open-...
-Search for Election district - there are quarterly updates to the centerline file so you will see four versions of all the district boundary files available for each year (i.e. Election District for 2014 will have a 14A, 14B, 14C & 14D version available).

tickets.question:
Hello,

The stop, frisk, and search data from 2017 to 2022 include “STOP_WAS_INITIATED”. The column includes three elements: Based on Self Initiated, Based on Radio Run, and Based on C/W on Scene.

Based on my understanding, each element can be defined as below.
Based on Self Initiated – Police officers initiated police stops without a warrant in hand.
Based on Radio Run – Police officers engaged in police stops after communicating with dispatchers.
Based on C/W on Scene – Police officers engaged in police stops after communicating with cooperating witnesses on scene.

Question1: Would you please confirm whether my understandings are correct? If possible, would you provide any document that includes more detailed information on each element?

The stop, frisk, and search data prior to 2017 do NOT include “STOP_WAS_INITIATED” but instead include the “radio” column (Yes/No).
Question 2: Is “Yes” equivalent to “Based on Radio Run” in the 2017-2022 data? Does "No" indicate “Based on Self Initiated” and “Based on C/W on Scene” in the 2017-2022 data?

Thank you for the help.
tickets.reply:
Question 1: Would you please confirm whether my understandings are correct? If possible, would you provide any document that includes more detailed information on each element?

Your assessment of the data variables are mostly correct, but there are many facts and circumstances that may lead a police officer to conclude that there is reasonable suspicion that a person has committed, is committing or is about to commit a felony or Penal Law misdemeanor. Such factors may include information received from third parties as well as the actions of the suspect, the suspect’s physical and temporal proximity to the scene of a crime, the suspect’s resemblance to the specific description of a perpetrator of a crime (based on more than just race, age and gender) and information known to the officer about the suspect or particular location, among other factors. Each situation is unique and the information available to members of the service will vary.


Question 2: Is “Yes” equivalent to “Based on Radio Run” in the 2017-2022 data? Does "No" indicate “Based on Self Initiated” and “Based on C/W on Scene” in the 2017-2022 data?

The SQF data prior to 2017 contains 2 data variables that can be used to gather additional information regarding the source of the information for a stop. Column #42 "radio" has a value of 'Y' or 'N' which indicates whether the stop was based upon a call from the police dispatcher. Column # 43 "ac_rept" has a value of 'Y' or 'N" which indicates whether the stop was based upon a report by a victim, witness or a police officer.



Thank you,
NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question: Does the building permit application dataset include permits for hoists? If so, how are they coded? If not, where can I find permits for hoists?
tickets.reply:
We have just updated the way we handle open data customer service, and your question from June was forwarded to me.

You are trying to find permits for hoists. This isn't something that we regularly report on, so it's not a simple thing. Here's how you can do it:

First, look for the job applications that include hoist equipment in our DOB Job Application Filings dataset by filtering the Job Description field for "hoist". This field is typed in by the applicant and there is no standardization, so you may want to make your filter narrower by specifying a type of hoist, but you might be excluding jobs where they didn't specify the type, so you'll have to play with this filter until you are satisfied with the results.
Use the Job # field from your filtered dataset in step 1 and cross reference with the DOB Permit Issuance dataset. Note: In the permit dataset, you may get several permits for a single Job #. You should look at the Work Type and Permit Type fields to narrow down to the exact permit that you want. For example, the entire alteration job might include both hoist equipment and scaffolds, and you don't want the SF (Scaffold) Permit Subtype.
That should get you to the report that you are looking for. If you have any additional questions, please let me know.

tickets.reply:
You are right: Job # is the key that should match these two datasets (DOB Job Application Filings and DOB Permit Issuance). Here are some parameters that will help troubleshoot this:

All permits should be connected to a job.
The jobs dataset only goes back to about 2014, and permits may be issued for jobs that are older.
Only jobs that have a status of Q, R, U, or X will have permits.
We are in the midst of applying a refresh to these datasets to correct an issue where Status was not updating. Permits should now provide updates whenever the permit status changes. Jobs should be fixed by the end of the year.
If you apply those parameters, you shouldn't see any permits without jobs. You can also check specific use cases by looking up the job or permit # in our Buildings Information System (BIS).

If you still have questions or still find anomalies, please let me know.

Thank you,

You can filter most datasets on the open data portal by date. For today's data in our DOB Job Application Filings dataset, the field you would use depends on what you mean by "today's data". (Note that this dataset updates daily with yesterday's data, so there will be a delay on "today".)

tickets.question:
Subject: DOB BIS Open Data: first-permit dates, fire-alarm coverage, and historical application records

Hello NYC Open Data / DOB data team,

Could you route this inquiry to the DOB data steward for these datasets?

• DOB Job Application Filings (ic3t-wcy2)
  https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/ic3t-wcy2
• DOB Permit Issuance (ipu4-2q9a)
  https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/ipu4-2q9a

We are investigating whether public building records can support research on permitting delays. Before modeling, we need to establish whether an application received its first permit within 90 calendar days of filing.

Our November 5, 2026 extract contains 66,708 legacy BIS A2/document-01 application rows with 2019 pre-filing dates, representing 51,608 job numbers, and 94,468 associated permit rows across all documents and dates. DOB NOW is outside this cohort. We recognize that these are current records about historical applications and that a missing match does not establish rejection or delay. No model has been trained.

Could you clarify the following, or point us to existing documentation?

1. Fire-alarm coverage and eligibility. All 3,008 fire-alarm-only jobs in our extract have no associated permit rows. Some nevertheless have a fully_permitted date; for example, job 302585735/document 01 shows 2019-04-23. What event does that field represent for these filings, and where should the corresponding authorization be found? How should pre-transition filings and jobs affected by the June 2019 FDNY transition be linked and classified? Our appendix includes five fire-alarm examples and one non-fire-alarm example, 321933690.

2. Original issuance and coverage. Does issuance_date on an INITIAL record preserve the original issuance after reissue, renewal, correction or replacement? How does it relate to BIS's First Issue Date and permit sequence 01? Are earlier, voided, rescinded, deleted or superseded events omitted or overwritten? What coverage limitations must be considered before interpreting absence of a permit within a 90-day window, including system migrations or missing historical events?

3. Filing origin and linkage. Which field corresponds to completed application filing: pre__filing_date, fully_paid, or BIS's Date Filed? For job 340689446, using pre-filing versus fully_paid changes the observed interval from 134 to 78 days. What is the correct application unit and join key across document and work-type permits? How should different job_s1_no records for the same job/doc, different dobrundate values, and repeated permit work/sequence combinations be interpreted? Job 123769751 has conflicting pre-filing dates across records.

4. Historical records. Are original application versions, dated amendments, archived exports, or event histories available? We need to establish what cost, work scope and other attributes were known at filing, and eventually distinguish review waiting time from applicant revisions, payments and other processing steps. Please identify available records, identifiers, effective/update dates, coverage, and the appropriate access route. If feasible, existing histories for the 11 appendix cases, from original filing through November 5, 2026, would help us test the definitions before seeking a larger extract.

The case appendix separates extract-only observations from BIS-page corroboration. Seven sampled BIS histories agree with our extracted first-issue dates, but this is partial review of the same underlying system, not proof of complete coverage. We have not treated unmatched cases as negative outcomes or later attributes as filing-time predictors.

The 11-case appendix is available on request; this form has no attachment field.

A documentation link, written field definitions, or referral to the appropriate DOB/FDNY data owner would be helpful. Please advise if a separate records request is needed for the historical material. We do not need personal contact details.

Thank you.

All permits should be connected to a job.

Hello NYC Open Data / DOB data team,

We are investigating whether public building records can support research on permitting delays. Before modeling, we need to establish whether an application received its first permit within 90 calendar days of filing.

Our November 5, 2026 extract contains 66,708 legacy BIS A2/document-01 application rows with 2019 pre-filing dates, representing 51,608 job numbers, and 94,468 associated permit rows across all documents and dates. DOB NOW is outside this cohort. We recognize that these are current records about historical applications and that a missing match does not establish rejection or delay. No model has been trained.

Could you clarify the following, or point us to existing documentation?

1. Fire-alarm coverage and eligibility. All 3,008 fire-alarm-only jobs in our extract have no associated permit rows. Some nevertheless have a fully_permitted date; for example, job 302585735/document 01 shows 2019-04-23. What event does that field represent for these filings, and where should the corresponding authorization be found? How should pre-transition filings and jobs affected by the June 2019 FDNY transition be linked and classified? Our appendix includes five fire-alarm examples and one non-fire-alarm example, 321933690.

2. Original issuance and coverage. Does issuance_date on an INITIAL record preserve the original issuance after reissue, renewal, correction or replacement? How does it relate to BIS's First Issue Date and permit sequence 01? Are earlier, voided, rescinded, deleted or superseded events omitted or overwritten? What coverage limitations must be considered before interpreting absence of a permit within a 90-day window, including system migrations or missing historical events?

3. Filing origin and linkage. Which field corresponds to completed application filing: pre__filing_date, fully_paid, or BIS's Date Filed? For job 340689446, using pre-filing versus fully_paid changes the observed interval from 134 to 78 days. What is the correct application unit and join key across document and work-type permits? How should different job_s1_no records for the same job/doc, different dobrundate values, and repeated permit work/sequence combinations be interpreted? Job 123769751 has conflicting pre-filing dates across records.

4. Historical records. Are original application versions, dated amendments, archived exports, or event histories available? We need to establish what cost, work scope and other attributes were known at filing, and eventually distinguish review waiting time from applicant revisions, payments and other processing steps. Please identify available records, identifiers, effective/update dates, coverage, and the appropriate access route. If feasible, existing histories for the 11 appendix cases, from original filing through November 5, 2026, would help us test the definitions before seeking a larger extract.

The case appendix separates extract-only observations from BIS-page corroboration. Seven sampled BIS histories agree with our extracted first-issue dates, but this is partial review of the same underlying system, not proof of complete coverage. We have not treated unmatched cases as negative outcomes or later attributes as filing-time predictors.

The 11-case appendix is available on request; this form has no attachment field.

A documentation link, written field definitions, or referral to the appropriate DOB/FDNY data owner would be helpful. Please advise if a separate records request is needed for the historical material. We do not need personal contact details.

Thank you.

tickets.question: I'd like to know more about the data collection process. Is this reported by the pantries/kitchens? And to confirm, this is report is duplicative (i.e., individuals may be counted as many times as they visit a pantry/kitchen)?
tickets.reply:
Both the ‘individuals served’ at food pantries and the ‘meals served’ at soup kitchens are self-reported and reflect the duplicated persons served by CFC-funded programs:
1. The number of individuals served by CFC-funded food pantries represents the total served by the food pantry based on the family size. This figure is duplicated meaning that individuals served are counted more than once depending on the number of visits. For example, if one person is picking up a pantry bag for a family of four, the pantry will record that four individuals were served. If that same family received another pantry bag that month, the pantry would record that eight individuals were served, etc. 
2. Soup kitchens are able to convert persons served to meals as each individual served represents one meal; again, this is a duplicated figure as an individual can be served at a soup kitchen multiple times in a month. 
 
The number of individuals served at food pantries and meals served at soup kitchens are reporting the same ‘Total Service’ measure that reflects the number of duplicated individuals served in a month, with pantries using the family size to count the number served and the soup kitchens counting the number of meals/individuals served.

tickets.question:
Hello,
My team at *****, a non-profit community development organization, is interested in using MapPluto data for a web mapping tool.
We have a few questions:
1. Are there notifications or change logs available for data updates regarding the MapPluto dataset, or would we need to manually check for updates?
2. Regarding the Restful API for MapPluto:
    - Do breaking changes result in a new version of the API, and is the API backwards compatible?
    - Are there notifications or timeframes provided when versions of the API are deprecated, and how long will deprecated versions continue to work?
    - Are email updates available when new data is released?
Thank you for your assistance.
Best regards,
*****
tickets.reply:
We received your inquiry from the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. Our response is as follows:
Below are the Department of City Planning’s (DCP) responses to your questions in bold:
1. Are there notifications or change logs available for data updates regarding the MapPluto dataset, or would we need to manually check for updates?
1. Notifications: There are not notifications for updates to our data on BYTES of the BIG APPLE. If you are comfortable with using REST services or ArcGIS online feature services, you could stream the data live so whenever we update the data your stream would be updated.
2. Change Logs:
    a. PLUTO Readme file explains changes to how the PLUTO file is generated between releases, if applicable.
    b. PLUTO CHANGE FILE README documents DCP applied changes to selected source field values.
 
2. Regarding the Restful API for MapPluto: To clarify, the RESTful API for MapPLUTO is an ArcGIS online feature service.
   - Do breaking changes result in a new version of the API, and is the API backwards compatible? When DCP updates the feature service for a new release of MapPLUTO (i.e. 24v2) the URL of that feature service is NOT changed.
   - Are there notifications or timeframes provided when versions of the API are deprecated, and how long will deprecated versions continue to work? No, the feature service is never deprecated unless Arcgis.com is unavailable.
   - Are email updates available when new data is released? No
Best,
Department of City Planning (DCP)

tickets.reply:
The ACRIS data in Open Data is updated each month (as noted this update is typically on the 8th of each month), but each update contains documents either recorded or corrected in the previous month. Thank you,
- NYC DOF

tickets.question: Is there any possibility to get all 4 million records? I use Xquery but it is limited to bring only 1000. Is there any possibility to get with out restriction ?
tickets.reply:
By default, the API returns a maximum of 1,000 records per request. To retrieve more than that, you can use the following techniques:
- Increase the Limit: You can increase the number of records returned by using the $limit parameter. For example, to request 50,000 records, you would use the following query: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/abcd-1234.json?$limit=50000 
- Paginate Using $offset: To request additional records, pair $limit with $offset to paginate through the data. This will allow you to pull the data in smaller batches:  
    - First Page: ?$limit=50000&$offset=0  
    - Second Page: ?$limit=50000&$offset=50000  	
- Optimize Your Query: Before making large requests, it's helpful to filter your results using the $select, $where, and $order parameters. This reduces unnecessary records and improves query performance.  
For more information on query parameters and how to work with large datasets please consult the following articles:  
- The LIMIT Clause 
- How to Query More Than 1000 Rows

tickets.question:
Hello! I have some questions regarding deed records in the "real property master" dataset. For context, I am grouping these records by bbl using "real property legals" and also joining party information using "real property parties":

- Why are there sometimes multiple deeds filed on one day for a given tax lot?
- When the last deed transaction date shows multiple deeds filed on the same day, how can we determine the current property owner of the tax lot?
- What does a 'docamount' value of 0 on a deed signify, specifically when the deed is filed the same day as other deeds with non-zero 'docamount' values?
-  How are 'documentid' values ordered, if at all?
tickets.reply:
The answers are as follows:


Why are there sometimes multiple deeds filed on one day for a give tax lot?
This is the nature of property sales and is controlled by the buyers and sellers and not the Department of Finance so we would not be able to list all reasons. Note that there is no requirement to record a deed when the property sells although transfer taxes returns must still be filed. With that said two common occurrences are:
Flips where party A sells the property to party B who then sells the property to party C. By looking at the document dates on the two deeds you can tell how long B help the property and often that will imply what B did with the property.
Settlement of an estate. In this case party A passes away and leaves the property to party B. Party B then only records the deed associated with this transfer then he sells to party C immediately prior to the recording for the deed from B to C.

When the last deed transaction date shows multiple deeds file on the same day, how can we determine the current property owner of the tax lot?
Generally speaking one should order by the document date from newest to oldest, next by CRFN from highest to lowest and finally by document id from highest to lowest. Note that the document id ordering is only useful for documents without CRFN which are those documents recorded prior to 1/1/2003 and brought into ACRIS from systems pre-dating ACRIS.

What does a ‘docamount’ value of 0 on a deed signify, specifically when the deed is filed the same day as other deeds with non-zero ‘docamount’ value?
As noted in the Data Dictionary for the Real Property Master dataset, the Document Amount field is the “Total Consideration for Transfers and Principal debt or obligation for Mortgages”. For deeds you can think of the Document Amount as the sales price. With this in mind, a Document Amount of 0 means the property was transferred with any money changing hands. There can be many reason for a $0 consider, but normally it means the transfer is not an “arms-length” transaction among unrelated parties. The reason most commonly associated with multiple deeds recorded the same day, some of which have non-zero consideration, is the settlement of an estate as mentioned earlier. When party B inherits the property from party A, no money changes hand; however when B sells to C, it is for a non-zero amount.


How are ‘documentid’ values ordered, if at all?
   There are three formats of Document ID in ACRIS. These are:

YYYYMMDDsssssttt = the format of documents record since 1/1/2003 where YYYY is the 4 digit year, MM is the 2 digit month, DD is the 2 digit day, sssss is a 5 digit sequence number within a day and ttt is a 3 digit sequence number within an ACRIS transaction. Document IDs in this format are assigned when the document submitter prepares the documents for recording. Documents with common ACRIS cover page transaction number, YYYYMMDDsssss, are submitted together and recorded in the order specified by sss. There is no significance to the ordering of the ACRIS cover page transaction numbers. Two submitters could prepare the documents for recording on the same day so share the YYYYMMDD portion of the document id, but could actually submit and have their documents recorded weeks or even months apart.
FT_Bssssssssssss = the format of documents whose index data was converted to ACRIS from the system immediately pre-dating ACRIS. In this format FT_ prefix is fixed, B is the property borough and ssssssssssss is a sequence number that increases with recording date.
BK_Btttttttttttt = the format of older documents whose microfilm images where indexed and imported into ACRIS. In this format the BK_ prefix is fixed, B is the property borough and tttttttttttt is a sequence number that increases with recording date. Note that BK_ documents are older than FT_ documents.
With this in mind, ordering FT_ and BK_ Document IDs has significance, but ordering Document IDs staring with 20 does not. For documents wit …

tickets.question: Would it be possible in the future to include blocks and lots in NYC Open Data's ACRIS - Real Property Master? This would be extremely helpful!
tickets.reply:
Borough, block and lot for real property recordings are available in the ACRIS Real Property Legals dataset which can be linked to the ACRIS Real Property Master dataset via the DOCUMENT ID and GOOD THROUGH DATE. ACRIS recordings are split this way because for each document in the Real Property Master dataset, there may be multiple associated properties in the Real Property Legals dataset. In other words, the split reflects the one-to-many relationship between the Master and Legals datasets.

Thank you,
NYC Department of Finance (DOF)

Each document can cover more than one property so for each document record in the “ACRIS - Real Property Master” dataset there may be one or more property records in the “ACRIS – Real Property Legals” dataset. The one to many link between these datasets is via the DOCUMENT ID and GOOD THROUGH DATE fields which are common to both datasets.

Thank you,
NYC Department of Finance (DOF)

tickets.question: So some datasets you update daily, we want to be able to maintain this data on our end to fetch the freshest data. The API for fetching data only allows to fetch 1000 records at a time. Is there a way around that?
tickets.reply:
By default, the API returns a maximum of 1,000 records per request. To retrieve more than that, you can use any of the following techniques:  
1. Increase the Limit: You can increase the number of records returned by using the $limit parameter. For example, to request 50,000 records:  https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/abcd-1234.json?$limit=50000 
2. Paginate Using $offset: To request additional records, pair $limit with $offset to paginate through the data:  
    a. First Page: ?$limit=50000&$offset=0  
    b. Second Page: ?$limit=50000&$offset=50000  
					(This will allow you to pull the data in chunks.) 
1. Optimize Your Query: Before making large requests, it's helpful to filter your results using the $select, $where, and $order parameters. This reduces unnecessary records and improves query performance.  
For more information on query parameters and how to work with large datasets please consult the following articles:  
- The LIMIT Clause Documentation (https://dev.socrata.com/docs/queries/limit.html)
- How to Query More Than 1000 Rows (https://support.socrata.com/hc/en-us/articles/202949268-How-to-query-more-than-1000-rows-of-a-dataset)

ACRIS Personal Property Parties can only be linked to other ACRIS Personal Property datasets. If you would like Master and Legals data corresponding to the records in the ACRIS Personal Property Parties dataset, link to the ACRIS Personal Property Master and ACRIS Personal Property Legals datasets respectively.

ACRIS data in Open Data is split into Real Property Documents and Personal Property documents where Real Property Documents are documents like deeds, mortgages, agreements and so on while Personal Property Documents are documents like UCCs and federal liens.

Documents with Class Code Description DEEDS AND OTHER CONVEYANCES, MORTGAGES & INSTRUMENTS or OTHER DOCUMENTS are Real Property Documents. NYC Department of Finance (DOF)

tickets.reply:
Queens 7A is not a community board district but is still a part of Queens 7.

The Queens 7A designation is for DSNY administrative reasons because we have a Mechanical Broom Garage with some other vehicles, like RO-RO trucks, that are allocated to that garage for a variety of collection activities for different material types.

tickets.question:

District 7A is not a geographic community district.  7A and districts like that are internal district notations where DSNY Broom Garages and other specialized equipment garages are located.  The tonnage however is part of the Master Community district.

Thank you,
- NYC Department of Sanitation

tickets.question:
I am requesting a change in the codes and categories used in the DSNY Monthly Tonnages dataset, a long-standing and widely used resource for understanding New York City’s waste generation and collection patterns.
In June 2025, there were revisions to this dataset to expand the range of collection types included in the Refuse, Paper, and MGP recycling categories. While broader reporting is welcome, the aggregation of Schools and Containerized/Special collections with Curbside collections into single lump-sum columns has reduced the dataset’s utility for both Open Data users and policymakers. Documentation of this problem is attached.
The proposed solution is straightforward: restore separate columns for Curbside, Schools, and Containerized/Special collections across all four material streams. This approach would:
- Align with DSNY’s existing internal reporting codes;
- Provide consistency across material categories; and
- Remain compatible with aggregated totals reported in other DSNY publications, including the Annual Report, Mayor’s Management Report, Zero Waste updates, and Solid Waste Management Plan documents.
- Preserve the agency’s goal to “to align with other DSNY published reports.”

Specifically, the curbside refuse should be code 01, Household Collection. School refuse should be code 81, School Trucks. And containerized other refuse should be all other codes. Curbside paper recycling should be code 31, school truck paper should be code 48, and all other codes should be containerized other paper. MGP tons should be code 33 for curbside, code 78 for school truck MGP, and all other MGP codes in containerized other.   Organics codes and categories are fine as is and don't need changes.
                    
Maintaining this level of detail is critical for accurate analysis, informed policymaking, and transparent public reporting. I appreciate NYC Open Data’s commitment to providing high-quality, actionable datasets, and believe the adjustments proposed here will enhance the value of DSNY Monthly Tonnages for all stakeholders.
Rationale:
1.     Under current aggregated reporting, calculating a capture rate for the curbside composting program, which is the nation’s largest and vastly outweighs schools or other small organics programs, is no longer possible because we can’t isolate curbside refuse tonnages in the denominator.  The same argument applies to curbside paper recycling and curbside MGP recycling capture rates.  
2.     Blending school tonnages with curbside and containerized tonnages prevents evaluation of school recycling and organics.  While I understand that not all schools are served only by school trucks for all streams, there is public value in reporting school truck collections, as evidenced by DSNY’s continuing reporting of school organics tonnages.
3.     The current method of reporting blends containerized collection data with school and curbside, making it impossible to track the progress of this distinct method of collection.

Thank you for your consideration. I look forward to your response and am happy to provide further clarification or examples if needed.
Respectfully submitted,
*****
For the months to 2002/07 to 2003/06, DSNY has listed MGP tonnages, and then reproduced those exact MGP tonnages again as "other organics" tonnages.  I assume this is an error?

I submitted a request in November 2025 for disaggregated reporting of DSNY tonnage data—specifically, four (4) separate monthly tonnage categories by sanitation district (curbside, containerized, school truck, and other), with each category reported across all four streams (refuse, paper, MGP, and organics).

At present, refuse, paper, and MGP tonnages are reported as lump sums that combine these distinct sources. This issue has been raised by the Manhattan Solid Waste Advisory Board and by former City Council Sanitation Chair Sean Abreu, including in at least one Council hearing, and is also of interest to members of the press.  Among other effects, the lump sum approach produces lower calculable diversion and capture rates than would be observed under a disaggregated framework that isolates curbside collections. My original request included documentation outlining both the need for this data and the analytical basis for disaggregation.  I understand, to a degree, the reluctance to disaggregate based on more containerization of refuse than recycling; and no containerization of organics, and the effects on the denominator.   However, this approach obscures important information that was previously public.

To date, I have received no response. I have also heard informally that DSNY does not intend to implement this request. If that is the case, I respectfully request a formal response explaining the decision, with a level of detail commensurate with the original submission.

If the reluctance reflects operational changes—such as increased containerization of refuse in some districts or changes in school truck collection—I would welcome clarification on how these changes are currently represented in reported tonnage totals. My review of trends by material code in FOIL-released data suggests that such shifts may be relevant, but they are not transparent in the current dataset.

If DSNY has agreed to implement the request, in whole or in part, I would appreciate confirmation and information on the expected timeline for implementation.
Respectfully submitted,
***

tickets.question:
‘firstname’ & ‘lastname’ variables are case sensitive. Pair that with the fact that the assigned registrationcontactid for a given contact is building-specific, and you leave next to no ability for people to consolidate the actions of a registered agent across buildings, and you leave developers open to the margin of error that comes with two individuals having the same name.
Let’s also discuss the fact that some registered agents use “johN doE” “j doe” “J DOE” “JOHN DOE” “John doe” “john Doe” “john doe”…  and so on in order to hide their affiliations and behaviors as registered agents at other specific properties. This is a MASSIVE error.. if it was even accidental in the first place.. it teeters on a violation of the Housing Maintenance Code, which specifically states that information in these registrations cannot be misleading or inaccurate. Implement case insensitivity, and even fuzzy matching. Assign ONE unique registrationcontactid to ONE unique individual. As it stands, the registrationcontactid serves no purpose. The registered agent of my building has 30+ different ones. One for each building. That defeats the purpose. Thankfully, I was able to consolidate data on my private server and implement the things that I am suggesting. The result? Game changing. I am able to see all LLCs that my landlord is associated with, all BINs — so all buildings. I then query the HPD Violations dataset and am able to see how many violations all of their buildings have, how many are open, closed, what class they are, and how long they have been letting them go.

For some perspective here: 
- I am a college dropout. 
- You are the government. 
- One of us makes a living helping small businesses make videos for social media.
- One of us collects their income through taxes.

The fact also that I need to report this is in-and-of-itself horrifying.

Warmest regards,
*****
tickets.reply: Thank you for your suggestions regarding property registration. We will review what technology changes are necessary and feasible at this time to make our data as user-friendly as possible for the purposes of analysis and grouping. We appreciate that this information is widely used and can provide valuable insight into conditions across buildings.

tickets.question:

I have a question for the collisions with ride sharing cars.
Where the ride sharing cars like Uber and Lyft are included in the vehicle type code?
I want to know the exact definition of the codes, especially 'livery vehicle', 'small com veh', 'passenger vehicle' and the differences among them.

Thank you in advance.
tickets.reply:
Uber/Lyft drivers who have a TLC license would be included in the Livery category, but certain ride types licensed in surrounding states would not need a TLC license to operate, therefore they would fall into the regular categories depending on the vehicle type if involved in a crash.

a) SEDN – Passenger Vehicle
b) SUBN – Sport utility vehicle/station wagon
c) VAN – Van
d) PICK – Pick-up Truck
e) SCOM – Small commercial vehicle (four tires) (e.g., box truck, etc)
f) LCOM – Large commercial vehicle (six or more tires) (e.g., semi, tractor-trailer, etc.)
g) TAXI – Taxi vehicle
h) LIV – Livery vehicle
i) BUS – Bus
j) AMBU – Ambulance
k) FIRE – Fire truck
l) MCY – Motorcycle
m) SCOOT – Scooter
n) BIKE – Bicycle
o) PCAB – Pedicab
p) UNK – Unknown
q) OTH – Other

Thanks,
NYC Open Data

tickets.reply:
Thank you for your question. The procedure is as follows: First a vehicle category must be selected from the following eight choices: 1. ATV, 2. Bicycle, 3. Car/SUV, 4. Truck/Bus, 5. Motorcycle, 6. tickets.question: Does each record pertain to a collision involving at least one motor vehicle?

To answer your question...
The Motor Vehicle Collisions crash table contains details on the crash event. Each row represents a crash event. The Motor Vehicle Collisions data tables contain information from all police reported motor vehicle collisions in NYC. The police report (MV104-AN) is required to be filled out for collisions where someone is injured or killed, or where there is at least $1000 worth of damage (https://www.nhtsa.gov/sites/nhtsa.dot.gov/files/documents/ny_overlay_mv-104an_rev05_2004.pdf). It should be noted that the data is preliminary and subject to change when the MV-104AN forms are amended based on revised crash details.For the most accurate, up to date statistics on traffic fatalities, please refer to the NYPD Motor Vehicle Collisions page (updated weekly) or Vision Zero View (updated monthly).

Thank you,
- NYC Open Data Team

For the years 1980-1998 I am scraping the data from hard copies of the Proceedings of the Council of the City of New York that are available at the Municipal Archives. But I am not sure if these two sources are reporting the same data. The Open Data database is clearly reporting meetings by the whole council, committees, and subcommittees. But I am not sure if the hard copies of the Proceedings are reporting subcommittee meetings. And perhaps there are other differences. My question is: Where did the data reported in the NYC Open Data database come from? If you got your data from the Proceedings hard copies, than the data I scrape from those sources may be of the same type as the data reported in the database you provided. But if your database came from a source other than the Proceedings hard copies, the data I scrape from there may not be comprable with the data your database provides. Please explain the source of your data and how you complied it so I answer this question. Thanks. Prof. XX
tickets.reply:
Hi Prof. Main, 

The Open Data set you reference is not scraped from the hard copies, it is directly input to the Legistar system. That dataset is maintained by our Legislative Records team, who coordinate the scheduling and tracking of meetings, minutes and legislation, and input everything to the Legistar database.

My understanding (from asking around for pre-Legistar institutional knowledge) is that the Proceedings of the Council are the collected minutes of all meetings.

Hope that's helpful,
Anne

tickets.question:
1. I wonder why most rows of the 'Fluoride' column have missing values(empty string). Does it mean those sites have 0 Fluoride?

2. Can you explain more on the 'Sample.Class'? What's the difference of 'Compliance' and 'Operational'? And what does the 'Resample' ones mean?

Thanks!
tickets.reply:
To answer your questions in order:

1. No. Only a subset of the daily samples are analyzed for Fluoride which include the entry points to the distribution system. The other sites/samples are Not Analyzed but are assumed to have similar levels to the values found at the entry points.
2. As stated in the Data Dictionary, copied below, not all data are used for Compliance. The other data are collected for Operational purposes but results are provided in OpenData. As required by the Total Coliform Rule, when a sample is positive for coliform at a Compliance site a set of Resamples must be collected from the location. For Operational sites it is only one resample.

Please note: Data are collected under the federal Revised Total Coliform Rule (RTCR) for compliance. All samples are collected and analyzed by DEP staff from fixed sample stations throughout drinking water distribution system. Data are used to assess the effectiveness of drinking water treatment in accordance with the requirements of federal and state rules and regulations. But not all data presented are used to determine / calculate compliance with the regulations.

Thank you,
- NYC DEP Open Data

tickets.question:
Hello! I am trying to get counts of boilers with certain types of primary fuel (e.g. No. 6, No. 4, No. 2, etc.) for each year, and I am a little confused which values I should be looking for in the dataset.
In particular, I am not sure if I should be counting boilers with "CANCELLED" permit statuses. Likewise, I am unsure if I should be excluding request types like "registration inspection" or "work permit" in my counts.
Any insights here or an updated data dictionary would be very helpful! Unless I am missing something, the dictionary on the site appears not to include certain values.
tickets.reply:
For Fuel Type – Primary and Secondary Fuel columns (both columns should be used to determine fuel type)
Boilers with “cancelled” should not be counted.
Request Type –
            Registration – boilers that are  0.35 to less than 2.8 MMBtu/hr
            Registration II and Registration Inspection – boilers that are 2.8 to less than 4.2 MMBtu/hr
            Work Permit and Certificate to Operate – boilers that are 4.2 MMBtu/hr and greater
Thank you,
NYC DEP Open Data

tickets.reply:

Based on the metadata provided:
Hurricane Evacuation Zones are determined by New York City Emergency Management and represent varying threat levels of coastal flooding resulting from storm surge. Hurricane evacuation zones should not be confused with flood insurance risk zones, which are designated by FEMA and available in the form of Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs).
For additional information we recommend reaching out to the NYCEM.

You need to reach out to the NYC Emergency Management office. They created the Hurricane Evacuation zones and conducted the SLOSH model analysis.
We can mention that hurricane categories do not have a direct correlation with the evacuation zones, but the more severe the category of hurricane, the more potential of impact on more evacuation zones. Superstorm Sandy was not even categorized as a hurricane when it reached NYC in 2012 but still impacted many of the evacuation zones.

tickets.agency: Financial Information Services Agency / Office of Payroll Administration (FISA-OPA)
tickets.question:
I have found 8k rows of data where the total gross pay is negative. I loaded the most recent data set (October 30 2024) and used the methodology from the data dictionary:
 total_ot_paid +total_other_pay + regular_gross_paid = total_gross_pay
If this is not an error, what explains negative payroll in the data?
tickets.reply: The negative salaries are not in error. There are various reasons for why there may be a negative salary, the most common reasons being check refunds (for example, due to overpayments made to the employee) and retroactive leave status changes. Please note that the citywide payroll dataset is organized by fiscal year, and changes may be made in the same calendar year, but the prior fiscal year, potentially impacting the total gross pay.

tickets.agency: Financial Information Services Agency / Office of Payroll Administration (FISA-OPA)
tickets.question:
Hi, when will the OPA Payroll dataset be updated with FY25?
Can this dataset be updated more frequently than once a year? As an example, as of August 2025 the data is 14 months out of date.
Thanks.
tickets.reply:
FY2025 will be added to the dataset at the end of October or at the beginning of November.
 
The fiscal year ends on June 30th each year, and thus cannot be updated before that date. The data analysis for citywide pay is conducted only after the fiscal year ends. The results must be reviewed by various agencies to ensure that information regarding every confidential employee is removed and/or redacted. The datasets for separate agencies must be then combined and hundreds of thousands of lines of data must be reviewed to ensure the integrity of the data is maintained. Data accuracy is also reviewed. The aforementioned process takes months. As such, it is updated only once a year.

tickets.question:
ubject: “Violation Status” Field and its relation to “Judgement Entry Date” field.
1- To which Violation status value “Judgement Entry Date” field is pertinent to?
(List of 15 “Violation status” we found in the data are: ADMIN CLAIM DENIED, ADMIN CLAIM GRANTED, ADMIN REDUCTION, APPEAL ABANDONED, APPEAL AFFIRMED, APPEAL MODIFIED, APPEAL REMANDED, APPEAL REVERSED, HEARING ADJOURNMENT, HEARING HELD-GUILTY, HEARING HELD-GUILTY REDUCTION, HEARING HELD-NOT GUILTY, HEARING HELD-REINSTATEMENT, HEARING PENDING, HEARING WAIVED)
2- Most of the data (about 75%) does NOT have a violation status, does this mean Violation Status field has a value only when a ticket is disputed?

3-Do you have “Violation status” workflow or Lifecycle?
tickets.reply:
1. There is no direct relationship between the JUDGMENT ENTRY DATE field and the VIOLATION STATUS field. The JUDGMENT ENTRY DATE field provides the date the violation entered into judgment status, which is based on a pre-determined penalty schedule. The VIOLATION STATUS field provides the status of a contested ticket, such as whether there is a hearing pending, or what the outcome of the hearing was. Hearings can take place both before or after the entry of judgment.

2. That is correct. Any uncontested ticket, whether it is ignored or paid, will have a blank VIOLATION STATUS.

3. There isn’t a set workflow associated with the VIOLATION STATUS values. All of the statuses, with the exception of ‘Hearing Pending’ reflect the outcome (or determination) from a hearing, whether it be an initial hearing or an appeal hearing. While there are common scenarios, the sequence of values for VIOLATION STATUS will depend on the specific case related to a disputed ticket. As an example, one common sequence might be…
‘Hearing Pending’ ---> ‘Hearing Held–Guilty’ ---> ‘Appeal Reversed’, which translates to a scenario in which a ticket was contested, found guilty at the initial hearing, and then dismissed at an appeal hearing. There are many other possibilities.

Thank you,
-NYC Department of Finance

tickets.question:
Can you explain how the penalty and interest amounts are calculated.
Please note that summons 1005796464 was opened on "2016-12-18 11:30:00" and has no interest but a $10 penalty charged, summons number 1102218753 written on "2017-02-08 15:58:00" has a penalty of $60 and an interest charge of $21.41.

tickets.reply:
​Thank you for contacting NYC Open Data Help Desk. The penalty amounts assessed in STARS depend on the type of violation. For camera violations, only one $25 penalty is assessed. For all parking violations, three penalties are assessed ($10, $20, and $30). The application of interest begins when a violation enters judgment status, and is calculated as 9% simple interest. As to the timing of penalty assessments and entry of judgment, there are different schedules depending on the category of plate a summons was issued to. Penalty assessments do not move beyond the first penalty on summonses for which the liable owner could not be determined (as is likely the case with the cited summons 1005796464).

The NYC Department of Finance has posted on its web site a section that describes Parking and Camera Violation Penalties and Enforcement Actions. Please refer to that page for additional information.

https://www1.nyc.gov/nyc-resources/service/7284/parking-and-camera-violation-penalties-and-enforcement-actions

- NYC Department of Finance

tickets.question:
I am requesting information re: the [Violation Status] field.

If there is a null value does that mean the recipient of the citation has not challenged the citation?

All the values that do appear in the [Violation Status] field seem to indicate hearings, appeals, or some other type of claim of the recipient of the citation.
tickets.reply:
“Yes, a null or blank value in the ‘Violation Status’ field indicates that the respondent has not contested the ticket.”

Below is a brief explanation of each of the possible values that may populate the ‘Violation Status’ field.

ADMIN CLAIM DENIED: Ticket was contested, and the claim was denied administratively, without an ALJ/hearing (contested - guilty)
ADMIN CLAIM GRANTED: Ticket was contested, and the claim was denied administratively, without an ALJ/hearing (contested - guilty)
ADMIN REDUCTION: Ticket was contested, and the claim was denied administratively, without an ALJ/hearing (contested - guilty)
APPEAL ABANDONED: Original guilty determination was appealed, but the respondent never followed through with the appeal hearing (contested - guilty)
APPEAL AFFIRMED: Original guilty determination was affirmed at an appeal hearing (contested - guilty)
APPEAL MODIFIED: Original guilty determination was affirmed at an appeal hearing (contested - guilty)
APPEAL REMANDED: Case deferred, similar to an adjournment (contested - no new determination…just the original guilty)
APPEAL REVERSED: Original guilty determination was reversed at an appeal hearing (contested - not guilty)
HEARING ADJOURNMENT: Ticket was contested, and brought to a hearing. The ALJ determined that more evidence was needed. Hearing was rescheduled for another day (contested - no determination yet)
HEARING HELD-GUILTY: Ticket was contested, and found guilty by an ALJ at a hearing (contested - guilty)
HEARING HELD-GUILTY REDUCTION: Ticket was contested, and found guilty by an ALJ at a hearing, with some reduction of previously assessed penalties (contested - guilty)
HEARING HELD-NOT GUILTY: Ticket was contested, and found not-guilty by an ALJ at a hearing (contested - not guilty)
HEARING HELD-REINSTATEMENT: Ticket was found guilty at a fraud hearing (previously dismissed fraudulently) and has been reinstated (contested - guilty)
HEARING PENDING: Ticket was contested, and hearing is pending (contested - no determination yet)
HEARING WAIVED: A settlement was agreed to by the respondent, which included a waiver of ever having a hearing (not contested)


Thank you,
- NYC Open Data Team

Use the FY2020 issuance dataset and search for speed camera violations in each month.
Parking Violations Issue Fiscal Year 2020: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Parking-Violations-Issued-Fiscal-Year-2020/pvqr-7yc4


The Open Parking and Camera Violations dataset is updated daily with status updates to existing violations in the dataset, new violations are added to the dataset on Sundays. A data set uploaded on Sunday will have data for up to the Thursday of that week which just ended.
To search for issuance in a specific month, use the referenced data set because the Open Parking and Camera dataset doesn’t support date range searches.
Open Parking and Camera Violation: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Open-Parking-and-Camera-Violations/nc67-uf89











Thank you,
- NYC DOF

tickets.reply:
Hello, to begin your query, I recommend visiting this guide on Exploration Canvas. It provides step-by-step instructions for filtering, grouping, and aggregating data—each of which will help you narrow down and analyze the dataset to find the information you’re looking for.

As a starting point, consider filtering by a specific date range. This will reduce the dataset size and make it easier to retrieve the most relevant data.

Unfortunately we are unable to create custom queries for users. But we did give your question an attempt and we got results. (screenshots shared)

Here are our instructions:
Visit the Dataset’s Main Page: Go to the Open Parking and Camera Violations dataset page: Open Parking and Camera Violations.

Navigate to the "Filter" Option (the funnel symbol): At the lower-left panel to the dataset, look for a button or tab with the funnel symbol. This is where you can start building custom views. It should be open on default
Add a Filter for the Violation Field:
- In the filter menu, locate the violation column.
- Typically, you’ll choose a “contains” filter or a similar option to match partial text.
- Set a filter to only include rows where violation contains the text "PHTO SCHOOL ZN SPEED VIOLA".
- Apply the filter.
Group the Data by violation_status:
- Then Look for an option to “Group” data (the box button under the funnel symbol).
- Select violation_status as the field to group by. This step will allow you to aggregate the data based on each unique violation status.
Add a Count for Each Group:
- Scroll from the group option down to "Aggregate by" 
- Select  violation_status as the column to use.
- Then open the  "Select calculation" options and choose count of rows
Apply the grouping and Review the Results:
- Apply the filters and grouping options, and the dataset will display a summary view.
- You should see a list of violation_status values, each with a count of records that meet the “PHTO SCHOOL ZN SPEED VIOLA” filter.
Export (Optional):
- If you need to save the filtered and summarized view, look for an Export option to download it in a format like CSV.

tickets.agency: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
tickets.question:
We consume Issued Licenses (w7w3-xahh, formerly "Legally Operating
Businesses") through the SODA API. Row data appears to have stopped
updating, while the dataset metadata still advertises "Update Frequency:
Weekly".

What we measured against the live API on 2026-08-16:

- rowsUpdatedAt is 2026-04-24; the newest license_creation_date in the
 dataset is 2026-04-16 — roughly four months of no new records.
- This is not an artifact of our filter. We grouped by license_status
 across the full vocabulary (Active, Expired, Surrendered, Failed to
 Renew, Ready for Renewal, Revoked, Voided, Suspended, Out of Business,
 Close, TOL) and no status has a record after 2026-04-16.
- The derived view pmxj-whmv ("Business Type - Based on Legally
 Operating Businesses") reports the identical rowsUpdatedAt of
 2026-04-24T19:30:43Z, which suggests the pause is upstream of the
 views rather than in any one of them.
- By contrast, License Applications (ptev-4hud) is current through
 2026-08-14, so DCWP publishing overall appears healthy.

One thing that may be worth flagging internally: the dataset page's
"Updated" timestamp currently shows 2026-08-14, because the view
metadata was modified then. Consumers watching that field would not
notice that the rows themselves are four months stale.

Could you confirm whether publication to this dataset is paused,
retired, or superseded? If it has been superseded, we would be glad to
know which dataset consumers should point to instead.

Thank you,
Sergey Kurilov
Zoningly

tickets.agency: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
tickets.question: I have a question about the Legally Operating Businesses dataset. Why is it so incomplete? For example, my database has over 160 companies in the Empire State Building at 350 5th Ave. However, I'm only seeing 8 licenses with that address when I filter. Can you help me understand the discrepancy? Thank you so much.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting NYC Open Data Help Desk.

The Legally Operating Businesses dataset is described as a dataset which, “… features businesses/individuals holding a DCA license so that they may legally operate in New York City.”
The Department of Consumer Affairs [DCA] does not count the number or types of businesses operating in non-licensed business categories.

A list of business categories licensed by the Department of Consumer Affairs can be found here: http://www1.nyc.gov/site/dca/businesses/licenses-apply.page
or downloaded as a PDF* here: http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/dca/downloads/pdf/businesses/licensing_industries_list.pdf

* Note: License categories appearing on pages one and two ONLY, of the PDF, are issued by Consumer Affairs. The license categories on pages three and four are issued by the NYC Department of Health & Mental Hygiene and do not fall under Consumer Affairs’ jurisdiction.

Thank you,
-NYC Department of Consumer Affairs

tickets.agency: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
tickets.question: I'm looking into business openings and closures in NYC. I was wondering if this is the right data set to look at the number of open businesses in New York City? The number of licenses seem far below the number of businesses in the city. Please let me know the appropriate data set to look at. Thanks!
tickets.reply:
Your request was referred to the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) for response.

DCWP does not possess any data that could reasonably be interpreted as inclusive of all businesses operating in the City.

The “Legally Operating Businesses” dataset is a list of licenses issued by DCWP.  Business activities requiring a DCWP-issued license are enumerated in Title 20, Chapter 2, of the NYC Administrative Code.

A current list of business activities requiring a DCWP-issued license can be found here, on the DCWP website (https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/dca/downloads/pdf/businesses/licensing_industries_list.pdf).

tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting the NYC Open Data Helpdesk! Your report was forwarded to the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) for review.

Applying for a DCWP-issued license is a matter of public record and that record is covered by NYC’s Open Data law. Consistent with DCWP’s Personally Identifying Information (PII) policy, other than name and the City, State, and ZIP Code of the mailing address, DCWP does not publish data regarding an individual’s contact information or address.

tickets.agency: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
tickets.question:
Hi there, I am hoping to better understand the capacity of parking garages in New York City. I am hoping you could clarify what types of properties are included in the data set. It appears that this is more than just parking garages. 

Only some of the lines mention "vehicle capacity" in the detail, and I see that some rows have "garage" for the industry. If I am hoping to see just parking garages, should I filter only rows for that are listed as "garage" for industry? What if I would like to see both surface lots and garages? 

It seems like some of these are businesses such as food vendors that may operate on lots but are not using the lots for parking. Any insights you could give would be helpful! 

Relatedly, do you know of any datasets that address average rates of utilization for garages? How full they tend to be? Thank you!
tickets.reply:
In 2023 DCWP combined three different business categories, “Garage”, “Parking Lot”, and “Garage & Parking Lot”, into a single “Garage & Parking Lot” business category. There is no longer any distinction in our systems. 
 
The dataset has been updated and the vehicle and bicycle capacity should be available in the “Details” column. 
 
DCWP does not maintain any data about the type of property where food vendors operate nor on utilization of parking garages.

tickets.agency: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
tickets.question:
Hi NYC Open Data Team,
I hope this message finds you well. I am reaching out regarding the Issued Business Licenses dataset (resource link).
It appears that geospatial fields (e.g., latitude, longitude, or property location) are missing from this dataset. It looks like only 'latitude' is listed as an attribute in the list of fields as well. These fields are essential for spatial analysis and visualization, particularly for organizations like Business Improvement Districts (BIDs) working to improve local economic conditions in partnership with city agencies.
Our team at *****, a Geo-CRM platform designed to support place management organizations, is actively helping NYC's BIDs enhance access to business license records and collaborate more effectively with city agencies. The inclusion of geospatial data in this dataset would greatly improve how these organizations analyze trends, manage resources, and plan for improvements.
Could the geospatial fields be added or updated to include location information associated with each license? Please let me know if additional information or clarification would be helpful.
Thank you for your time and for maintaining such a valuable resource for New York City.
Best regards,
*****
tickets.reply:
DCWP publishes address and location information for premises businesses and does not publish address or location information for individual licensees.
With regards to the attribute list, there are 31 fields in the dataset. If you scroll to the bottom of the attribute list on the “About” page and select 50 from the “Rows Per Page” drop-down, you will see latitude and longitude are both present in the list.

tickets.agency: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
tickets.question: I am looking to map the number of jobs or workplaces in New York at the most disaggregated unit possible. I saw on your website that you have the Count of SHADs by Borough - https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Business/Count-of-SHADs-by-Borough/sxds-xunb/about_data -  but I need the number of employees, rather than businesses, and per census tracks or blocks so that I can use GIS to map them. Do you have that information? Thank you
tickets.reply: DCWP does not track the number of employees for this category. Please refer to the "Issued Licenses" dataset on NYC Open Data (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Business/Issued-Licenses/w7w3-xahh/data_preview). This dataset contains address and geospatial data, and can be filtered for [Business Category] = "Secondhand Dealer - Auto" and [License Status] = "Active".

Also, how different are these 3 above-listed values from “IN VIOLATION” and what specifically does this mean? Are there overlaps in meaning?

Also, could you please enlighten me as to what the prefix “SAU” stands for in the scheduledhearinglocation and the decisionlocationborough variables. This prefix “SAU:” is placed before every borough. For example, “SAU: BKLN” or “SAU”MANH”.

Finally, I am not sure if this is a typo but in the violationdescription variable, besides “ASBESTOS”, “BAR”, “COMMERCIAL”, “FIRE”, “MULTIPLE DWELLING”, and “NOISE” there is the “1 -D142 2 FAMILY” value whose meaning I cannot fathom.

Thank you in advance for your time.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting NYC Open Data Help Desk. Please see below the responses to your questions:
​
​For the hearingstatus variable, I am unable to find any information as to what some of the terms mean:
While I am aware that “ASSIGNED” means “summons had a hearing, the case is assigned, and a decision is pending but do the following mean, exactly: “ASSIGNED TO APPEALS”; “HRG BEFORE ASSIGN”; “PERFECTION REQUIRED”; “STAY REQUESTED”; “STAYED”; and STIPULATION OFFERED. For the last one, specifically, what is the difference between “STIP NEEDS REVIEW” (which means “Stipulation offered by enforcement agency (petitioner) and stipulation was accepted by respondent”) and “STIPULATION OFFERED”?

Assigned – Assigned to a hearing officer.
Assigned to Appeals – the summons has had an appeal filed and is with our appeals department
Hrg before assign – the summons was heard before OATH got a copy of it
Perfection Required -- An appeal has been entered but there is still paperwork that needs to be filed for the appeal to progress
Stay Requested – the respondent has filed a request to stay a case and prevent it from progressing (to default/docketing/collections etc.)
Stayed – For a variety of legal reasons (e.g., a respondent request, a hold pending some kind of negotiation or legal case), the case has a stay placed on it
Stipulation offered – this is a program that allows certain Buildings cases to be settled before a hearing subject to certain conditions. This indicator means that the offer of stipulation was sent out by OATH on behalf of the issuing agency.
Stip needs review – A respondent has accepted the offer of stipulation but for a variety of reasons, the stipulation may require intervention by OATH staff in order to be processed

For the hearingresult variable, what does “COSRV INVIO” mean? Likewise for “POP IN-VIOL” and “SETTL IN-VIO”. I am unable to find any information on your website as to what they refer to. Also, how different are these 3 above-listed values from “IN VIOLATION” and what specifically does this mean? Are there overlaps in meaning?

​​COSRV INVIO means "In Violation, Community Service Eligible" and applies only to summonses related to the Criminal Justice Reform Act (CJRA), for which community service is an available alternative to payment of a fine for an In Violation summons.
POP In Vio means "In Violation – Publicly Owned Property" – the respondent is the city itself. In these cases, the agency that owns the property isn't required to pay.
Settl In Vio means that there was a settlement prior to hearing and the respondent is recorded as having been in violation as a condition of to that settlement
​They all mean that the finding is that the respondent is in violation.
​
​Also, could you please enlighten me as to what the prefix “SAU” stands for in the scheduledhearinglocation and the decisionlocationborough variables. This prefix “SAU:” is placed before every borough. For example, “SAU: BKLN” or “SAU”MANH”.

SAU signifies that a case was assigned to the Hearings by Mail unit
​
​Finally, I am not sure if this is a typo but in the violationdescription variable, besides “ASBESTOS”, “BAR”, “COMMERCIAL”, “FIRE”, “MULTIPLE DWELLING”, and “NOISE” there is the “1 -D142 2 FAMILY” value whose meaning I cannot fathom.

​This field is used by various agencies to store various information, generally indicating something additional (a building type, a violation type) – it’s not consistent across OATH’s data. I will contact Open Data to see how they're assembling it
​
Thank you,
-Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings

​b) Decision Printed - respondent signed out for the decision following the hearing.
​c) Batch Insert - summons was entered into NYCServ.

Please note that this dataset has recently undergone a major revision with additional summonses from DCA, DOHMH and TLC added. Agency is currently in the process of reviewing and correcting discrepancies.

tickets.agency: Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH)
tickets.question:
I am a data analysist for Jones Lang Lasalle and we have technicians operating in the NYC area who have received idling violations.
In an effort to be proactive and notify our technicians of new violations, I'm pulling data from the NYC Open Data OATH database. (OATH Hearings Division Case Status | NYC Open Data (cityofnewyork.us))

I'm filtering the data to our company and specifically idling violations.

I had a few questions around the NYC Open Data OATH and was hoping someone could help me. Below are my questions:
How long does it take for an idling violation to appear within the OATH NYC open data?
When looking at violations for idling, I'm seeing 5 fields that are charge/penalty fields, could someone help me understand how they total up?
Charge 1 Infraction amount
Additional Penalties or Late Fees
Penalty Imposed
Total Violation Amount
Balance Due

For example, summons number 000766944Y has the following values

Charge 1 Infraction amount = $350
Additional Penalties or Late Fees = $300
Penalty Imposed = $1,000
Total Violation Amount = $350
Balance Due = $1,300

I believe the Total Violation would be the sum total of charge 1 (or charge 2, 3 etc). Is this correct?
Assuming this is correct, Then the initial amount due would be $350. The "Additional Penalties or Late Fees" being $300, would now total up to $650.
Why is the "Penalty Imposed" at $1,000? And then the Balance Due = $1,300?

Wouldn't it be Total Violation Amount + Additional Penalties + Penalty Imposed = Balance Due?
Making this $350 + $300 + $1000 = $1650?

I'm just trying to understand the penalty and additional fee data from the NYC Open Data OATH data set so that we can account for the fees correctly.

My final question would be once a violation is paid; how long does it take to show "Paid" in the NYC Open Data OATH dataset?

Thank you for your help.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. The total balance of $1,300 on Open Data is correct. The face amount of violation totaling $350 increased to $1,000 at default (based on the default penalty schedule) when the respondent did not show up for the hearing. Thereafter, there were late fees at 10% ($100) for each month in arrears, presumably for 3 months, which totaled $300. Therefore, the total balance due of $1,300 is the total of the default amount for $1,000 and the late fees of $300.

Thank you,
NYC Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH)
