Excel does have limitations when handling large datasets, as it can only support up to 1,048,576 rows. Given the size of the dataset at the link you provided, we don’t recommend trying to download the entire dataset directly into Excel. Instead, we suggest filtering the data to around one million records or fewer per download to ensure compatibility with Excel.

Alternatively, downloading the data as a CSV file can be a more flexible option. However, please note that the full dataset in CSV format can be quite large, approximately 15.6 GB uncompressed. Even with a strong internet connection, download times can range from 20 to 50 minutes or longer, depending on factors like connection speed and server load. Also keep in mind that the export function waits for the data file to be whole and complete before showing up in your browsers download queue. on our end, we filtered the data to about 500,000 records and got a CSV to download in 3-5 minutes.

Please let us know of you continue to experience issues or would like additional assistance.

tickets.reply:
OATH Hearings open dataset is not categorizing summonses into specific groupings for hearing pool purposes. However, a respondent may have multiple summonses; therefore, it is possible to query the dataset by respondent name, which may return more than one summons. tickets.question:
I'm trying to map Sanitation Violations, a view based based on OATH Hearings Division Case Status , provided by the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) but there is no latitude/longitude georeference data. tickets.reply:
The Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) dataset does not include detailed geographic coordinates (e.g., latitude and longitude), as the respondent typically provides demographic and location data. However, the dataset does include violation ZIP codes.
A practical approach for users interested in mapping violations beyond ZIP code boundaries is to obtain an open-source ZIP code reference dataset that includes corresponding latitude and longitude values. By merging the OATH dataset's violation ZIP codes with this reference dataset, users can approximate geographic coordinates for mapping and spatial analysis. 
Here are several reliable and free open datasets that provide U.S. ZIP codes with corresponding latitude and longitude values to complement the OATH dataset for spatial analysis:
 
1. United States ZIP Code Database – SimpleMaps (Free Version)
- URL: https://simplemaps.com/data/us-zips
2. U.S. Census Bureau – Gazetteer Files
- URL:https://www.census.gov/geographies/reference-files/time-series/geo/gazetteer-files.html
3. GeoNames.org – U.S. ZIP Codes
- URL: https://download.geonames.org/export/zip/
4. Open Data Soft – U.S. ZIP Codes with Geo Data
URL:https://public.opendatasoft.com/explore/dataset/us-zip-code-latitude-and-longitude/

tickets.question:
Hi there,

I hope this message finds you well. I am a data analyst at HPD hoping to work with this dataset to identify properties that may be in potential physical distress. I see the charge codes, code sections, and code descriptions listed, but I wondering if you are aware of any resources which classify each code in terms of severity. For example, I found this resource (1_RCNY_102-01.pdf) which classifies each section of law as class 1, class 2, or class 3, but this is only a subset of the charges found in the OATH dataset, and is not easily joined to the OATH dataset. My hope would be to enrich this NYC open dataset with a severity classification column to better understand the distribution of charges by severity.

Thank you for your help,
XXX
tickets.reply:
Hi ***,
Thank you for your interest in the OATH Hearings Division Case Status dataset.
OATH does not assign or maintain a standardized severity classification for summonses. Because OATH adjudicates summonses issued by multiple agencies, each agency uses its own enforcement framework and classification system. As a result, there is no single reference table or field that classifies all OATH charge codes by severity.
Some agencies classify violations by severity, but the classification systems differ. For example, the Department of Buildings (DOB) uses Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3, while the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) uses Class A, Class B, and Class C. Other agencies do use different severity schemes, penalty schedules, and some without formal severity classification at all.
If you would like to classify violations by severity, you would need to obtain the applicable classification from the issuing agency based on the charge code or code section.
I hope this information is helpful. Please let me know if you have any additional questions.
Thank you.

OATH Hearings Division Case Status (jz4z-kudi): API answers from a copy stuck on 21 October

The API for OATH Hearings Division Case Status (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/jz4z-kudi) answers the same query from two different copies of the data, at random.

- One copy is current. Today it is the copy of Tue, 27 Oct 2026 05:08:12 GMT. It reports X-SODA2-Data-Out-Of-Date: false.
- The other copy is stuck on Wed, 21 Oct 2026 04:35:17 GMT. It reports X-SODA2-Data-Out-Of-Date: true.

With an app token, the SODA3 query endpoint names the server in the x-soda2-secondary header:
- pg.pg13-a-fedramp-prod: current. x-soda2-data-out-of-date: []
- pg.pg14-c-fedramp-prod: stuck. x-soda2-data-out-of-date: ["jz4z-kudi"]

How to see it:
Open https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/jz4z-kudi.json?ticket_number=080054246N and refresh it a few times. When pg13-a answers, you get the summons. When pg14-c answers, you get [] because that summons is not in the 21 October copy.

Today at 8:17 PM New York time, 10 SODA3 requests for this ticket: 7 came from pg13-a and 3 from pg14-c. Earlier today, the same query for 85 tickets, sent 20 times: 12 answers came from the 21 October copy and 8 from the newer copy.

Effect:
- A summons can show one status on one request and another status on the next (for example DOCKETED, then PAID IN FULL).
- Summonses added since 21 October are missing from part of the answers.
- On the website, the dataset can look "not updated" even when it is.

We first saw this on 26 October 2026.

Request: please re-sync pg.pg14-c-fedramp-prod for jz4z-kudi, or stop it from answering for this dataset. Please let us know when it is fixed.

Thank you.

tickets.question:
Subject: Request for archived NYC BUILDING releases and building-level floor area data for 2023–2024 research

Hello NYC Open Data team,

I am conducting an academic study of building electricity consumption and nighttime satellite radiance in New York City during January 2023–December 2024. The study requires the surrounding building stock, including buildings outside Local Law 84 reporting.

The BUILDING dataset page (3g6p-4u5s) states that previously posted versions are retained and can be provided upon request. Could you please provide, or direct me to:

1. Archived releases of BUILDING / Building Footprints immediately before January 2023, releases available during 2023 and 2024, and the release closest to the end of December 2024. Please retain the original release/extraction dates and version identifiers. Corresponding BUILDING_HISTORIC releases or change logs would also be helpful if available.

2. Original footprint geometry and attributes, particularly BIN, DOITT_ID, BASE_BBL, MAPPLUTO_BBL, HEIGHT_ROOF, feature code, construction/demolition/alteration information, and any available observation dates or valid-from/valid-to fields. GeoJSON, FileGDB, or shapefile ZIP is suitable. A citywide release is preferred; a dated archive is more useful than a current map.

3. An explicit statement of the vertical units used for HEIGHT_ROOF in these releases and the current BUILDING GeoJSON export, including whether units or field definitions changed. The published metadata describes height relative to ground but does not explicitly specify this field's unit. We also need to distinguish observation/physical-event dates from database edit dates.

4. Please route to the appropriate DOF/DCP data owner: is there a releasable 2023 baseline and 2024 comparison dataset of building-level gross floor area with a BIN–BBL crosswalk, including buildings on multi-building tax lots and buildings outside LL84? If RPAD/PTS/CAMA records can support this, please specify the dataset, version, tax/fiscal versus calendar year, area units/definition, and how individual building records reconcile to tax-lot totals. Parcel-level total floor area alone will not resolve allocation across multiple buildings.

We already have current BUILDING and BUILDING_HISTORIC GeoJSON, MapPLUTO 23v3.1 and 24v4.1, PAD23d, DOB/BIS and DOB NOW certificates of occupancy, permit datasets, and LL84 annual/monthly records. We are requesting historical releases and the missing temporal/unit/building-level evidence, rather than another copy of the current datasets.

If any requested fields or archives do not exist or cannot be released, please indicate which items are unavailable and whether an alternative authoritative source is available. We do not assume that a permit issue date, CO issue date, sign-off date, or database edit date is the date a physical building change occurred.

Thank you.

Subject: Request for archived NYC BUILDING releases and building-level floor area data for 2023–2024 research

Hello NYC Open Data team,

I am conducting an academic study of building electricity consumption and nighttime satellite radiance in New York City during January 2023–December 2024. The study requires the surrounding building stock, including buildings outside Local Law 84 reporting.

The BUILDING dataset page (3g6p-4u5s) states that previously posted versions are retained and can be provided upon request. Could you please provide, or direct me to:

1. Archived releases of BUILDING / Building Footprints immediately before January 2023, releases available during 2023 and 2024, and the release closest to the end of December 2024. Please retain the original release/extraction dates and version identifiers. Corresponding BUILDING_HISTORIC releases or change logs would also be helpful if available.

Original footprint geometry and attributes, particularly BIN, DOITT_ID, BASE_BBL, MAPPLUTO_BBL, HEIGHT_ROOF, feature code, construction/demolition/alteration information, and any available observation dates or valid-from/valid-to fields. 3. An explicit statement of the vertical units used for HEIGHT_ROOF in these releases and the current BUILDING GeoJSON export, including whether units or field definitions changed. The published metadata describes height relative to ground but does not explicitly specify this field's unit. We also need to distinguish observation/physical-event dates from database edit dates.

Please route to the appropriate DOF/DCP data owner: is there a releasable 2023 baseline and 2024 comparison dataset of building-level gross floor area with a BIN–BBL crosswalk, including buildings on multi-building tax lots and buildings outside LL84? Hello, my name is *****, and I am examining the dataset for my graduate school data science class. 
In this dataset, I believe the "RACE" column should encompass "Black", "White", "Asian", "Amer.Indian", "Other", and "Unknown". However, the current dataset only lists "Black", "Asian", and "Unknown". It seems unlikely that all inmate admissions fall into these three categories. Could the remaining categories be subsumed under "Unknown" for a particular reason? Or is it that there are genuinely no inmates from those categories? 
Your clarification would be greatly appreciated.

Hello, I am seeking clarification on the type of inmate the data represents. Initially, I assumed it pertained to inmates' admissions to prison; however, the data indicates that the duration of detentions is relatively brief, spanning only a few hours or days, leading to my confusion. Is it about inmates in prison? Or, any other facility?

Sincerely,
tickets.reply:
This data represents individuals admitted into the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. The Dept. of Correction serves to provide the care, custody and control of individuals awaiting trial or serving a sentence after being found guilty for misdemeanor charges (serving less than one year). This means the vast majority of persons in custody have not been found guilty of a crime and the conditions for their incarceration can change as their case is adjudicated.
 
Individuals awaiting a trial may leave the custody of NYC DOC for a variety of reasons. For example, individuals may pay bail for release, they may be extradited to another jurisdiction, or they may have charges dropped or revised, thus no longer requiring incarceration before trial.

After an Executive Budget has been released by the Mayor, it is reviewed and revised by the City Council. If approved by the Council, the budget becomes “adopted.” The Adopted Budget is then sent back to and released by the Mayor in June.

The current modified budget is the Adopted Budget as revised through modification and approval in accordance with the City Charter.

The financial plan is an adjustment of current year expenditures and revenue forecasts and a projection of how these adjustments will affect future budgets.
The financial plan is released four times a year - one in the fall/winter, the Preliminary in January, the Executive in April, and the Adopted Budget in June.

Which is the most up to date number for what the city actually spent in a given FY?

The City Comptroller publishes a Comprehensive Annual Financial Report which details annual spending for the City. This document is available on the City Comptroller’s website.


Thank you,
- NYC Office of Management and Budget

tickets.reply:
I'm not entirely sure I understand your question. By "commercial and multifamily development projects" I think you're asking about larger buildings. At DOB, we generally classify buildings as "1-3 Family" or "Other", so I think all you need is to find the "Other" buildings.

If you're looking for brand new construction, then you're right - you need to find New Building (NB) jobs. If you're only interested in jobs that are currently underway, use our DOB Permit Issuance dataset, and filter Permit Type for "NB", and Bldg Type for "2" (this will get you those "Other" buildings). If you're interested in jobs that have been submitted for approval, but may be in various stages of the approval process (including construction that is underway), then you should use our DOB Job Application Filings dataset. Filter Job Type for "NB" and Building Type for "OTHERS".

If you have additional questions, please feel free to contact me again.

Thank you,
DOB Open Data Coordinator

tickets.reply: Per the Open Data Law (https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/open-data-law/), users do not need a license in order to copy, reuse, or share the data on NYC Open Data. New York City's open data is free for anyone to use for any purpose they see fit. We do not require, but encourage users to cite the data and share the results under a similarly permissive license. Our team would love to see the results of your analysis! Once they're done, please submit any project that uses NYC Open Data to be featured on our Project Gallery (https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/projects/) via this submission form: https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/project-submit/.

tickets.question:
Dear NYC Open Data team and Department of Health and Mental Hygiene,

I'm building *** a free public website, still in development, that helps families read child care inspection records in plain language. Each provider's page shows what the city or state published (inspections, the rules cited, corrections), with the date and a link back to the official record.

New York City publishes its child care programs and their inspections in NYC Child Care Connect (a816-healthpsi.nyc.gov), and on NYC Open Data: the dataset gy3q-4tzp, licensed Public Domain and updated daily, lists 2,748 programs with their ages, capacity and location, including the day care centers the State's own dataset leaves out, while the open inspections dataset (dsg6-ifza) is no longer updated. NYC.gov's terms say "All rights are reserved" and send permission requests to the agency, so we have collected and shown nothing from New York City, and won't until we hear from you. Until then we also leave out the State's own records of programs in the five boroughs.

Could you tell me three things? First, whether we may publish the city's programs from the Public Domain dataset gy3q-4tzp alone, and nothing from Child Care Connect, unless DOHMH prefers otherwise; NYC Open Data's FAQ says "There are no restrictions on the use of Open Data". Second, whether DOHMH would resume updating the open child care inspections dataset (dsg6-ifza), or permit a once-a-day read of NYC Child Care Connect, at a gentle pace (one request a second at most, or slower if you prefer, with a User-Agent that names the project and gives its web address). Third, whether you'd like us to credit the records in a particular way.

How we'd use them: they would be free to read for everyone, with no account needed, and we never sell or license New York City's records. We name no people: organizations only, never staff, owners who are individuals, or home-based providers by their own name, and a home-based provider is shown by its city and ZIP code only. Every finding shows its date and links to your record, and anyone who believes a record is wrong is sent to your correction process. We may offer paid services built on other data (for example, federal nursing-home data), and optional conveniences such as change alerts, but New York City's records themselves stay free.

If automated reading isn't something you allow, I'll respect that. We'll show a note that New York City's records are on your site, with a link, rather than collecting them.

Thank you for your time.

***

tickets.question:
I would like to know why there are names and list numbers (for the same exam, Exam: 7005, COMPUTER SPECIALIST (SOFTWARE), with a total list size of 2,403 names) that show up on Civil Service List (Active) Dataset, but do not show up on the Civil Service List Certification dataset? found here:
https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Civil-Service-List-Certification/a9md-ynri/data

From own review, the only difference I can find between the two datasets are the names listed on the "Civil Service List Certification" dataset have been contacted by multiple NYC Agencies to attend a hiring pool (going by the "Request Date" and "List Agency Desc" fields).

There are people who are present on both the Active & Certification datasets who have been given "Request dates" on the "Civil Service List Certification" dataset who have a high list numbers (example list numbers: 2352, 2360, 2364, 2369, 2370, 2379, 2382, 2385, 2394, 2396, 2403). While there are list numbers present on the Civil Service List (Active) dataset with lower list numbers who are not listed at all on the "Civil Service List Certification" dataset (example: 476.5, 527.5, 606.5, 1073.5, 1163.5, 1358.5, 2226, 2237, etc...). Why is that?

In another case I've actually found a person with 1 list number displayed on the Civil Service List (Active) dataset (example: 1428.500,), but the same exact person has two list numbers (same exam: 7005) on the "Civil Service List Certification" dataset (example: 603.500 and 1428.500,) who appears to have been contacted multiple times recently for both list numbers to attend a hiring pool. Would someone from the NYC Open Data team be able to investigate the possible discrepancies and help clarify the differences between the two data sets?
tickets.reply:
You inquired concerning Exam No. 7005, Computer Specialist (Software), and the data for that exam on the Civil Service List and Civil Service List Certification datasets.

As you observed, the number of entries on the Certification dataset is substantially greater than the number of entries on the Civil Service List dataset, as a new record (row) is created each time an eligible candidate is included on a list certification to an agency.  A single eligible candidate may be called on numerous certifications/hiring pools during the lifetime of the list.

With respect to candidates on the eligible list whose names do not appear on any certifications, those candidates may have taken other jobs, withdrawn themselves for consideration, or may have been disqualified.  With respect to Mr. Delaude, his correct list number is 1428.5.

tickets.reply: In answer to your question, in instances where multiple candidates on an eligible list receive the same score, list numbers are assigned by using certain digits of each candidate's social security number.  When agencies request that candidates be certified, the names of all candidates with the same scores are provided as a "tie group".

tickets.question:
Dear DOI Open Data Coordinator,
Together with a group known as the ***, I’ve been working through the new Evictions dataset published by DOI for pending, scheduled, and executed evictions starting in 2017. I have a number of questions regarding the dataset that I would greatly appreciate any insight into:
1. We are interested in de-duplicating the dataset to measure aggregate evictions throughout the five boroughs , and there are a number of observations that have a) identical index & docket numbers or b) identical marshal name, address, date, and unit number. Do either the former or the latter indicate duplicate observations? In the former situation, it would make sense that a unique index & docket combination would refer to a unique eviction, as the index # seems to be a unique ID provided by NY Housing Court, and docket # seems to be a unique ID assigned by the marshal. However, there are cases of duplicate index & docket combination assigned to different eviction addresses, unit #s, etc. In the latter situation, we are not sure whether we can rule out the possibility of these duplicates referring to, for example, same-day evictions in different units in the same building (where a marshal might have just recorded one unit # for ease). Please advise on how we should be thinking of de-duplicating this dataset.
2. Does this dataset constitute the universe of eviction judgments in the five boroughs from the NY Housing Courts? In other words, are there examples where eviction judgments are determined for a certain tenant that goes through NY Housing Court where a Marshal’s eviction would not automatically be scheduled and thus recorded in this dataset?
3. Relatedly, in the ‘Schedule_Status’ column of the dataset, all ~38k observations are listed as ‘Scheduled’ (in the data dictionary the column is described as either having values ‘Scheduled’, ‘Pending’, or ‘Confirmed). Assuming this is a mistake, when can we expect an update to the data in this column?
4. The data come with addresses of variable accuracy and without geospatial information, which is in violation of Local Law 108 of 2015, which requires, “every public data set containing address information to utilize a standard field layout and presentation of address information and include corresponding community district and geospatial reference data.” When can standardized addresses and geospatial reference data be expected to be appended to the dataset?
Thanks very much for your engagement with the above questions – we are looking forward to hearing back.
Best,
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting NYC Open Data Help Desk. Please see agency's response below:
​
​1. We are interested in de-duplicating the dataset to measure aggregate evictions throughout the five boroughs, and there are a number of observations that have a) identical index & docket numbers or b) identical marshal name, address, date, and unit number. Do either the former or the latter indicate duplicate observations? In the former situation, it would make sense that a unique index & docket combination would refer to a unique eviction, as the index # seems to be a unique ID provided by NY Housing Court, and docket # seems to be a unique ID assigned by the marshal. However, there are cases of duplicate index & docket combination assigned to different eviction addresses, unit #s, etc. In the latter situation, we are not sure whether we can rule out the possibility of these duplicates referring to, for example, same-day evictions in different units in the same building (where a marshal might have just recorded one unit # for ease). Please advise on how we should be thinking of de-duplicating this dataset.
​
​The court assigns each eviction/legal possession case a unique index number. Docket numbers are assigned by a marshal’s office but one case may carry different docket numbers. For example, should the landlord instruct the marshal to request separate warrants for each of the respondents named in the case, each respondent will be entered as a separate docket. Some marshals add a letter “b or “c” to the docket number, which is an indication that there is more than one warrant of eviction associated to one index number. Also, an index number may be linked to different floors within the same address (Example, 2 or 3 family home occupied by an entire family or by unidentified squatters. In sum, one index number, with one or more docket numbers, is one or more eviction(s).
​
​Moreover, different county courts (Kings, Queens, Bronx, Manhattan and Richmond) may use the same index number used in other counties for different eviction cases. Some marshals may add the first letter of the corresponding county to indicate which borough it came from. In short, there can be one index number, for different addresses in different counties.
​
​2. Does this dataset constitute the universe of eviction judgments in the five boroughs from the NY Housing Courts? In other words, are there examples where eviction judgments are determined for a certain tenant that goes through NY Housing Court where a Marshal’s eviction would not automatically be scheduled and thus recorded in this dataset?

This dataset will never constitute the entire universe of “eviction judgments.”

Petitioners may obtain a court ordered judgment of eviction and, through later negotiations among the parties, the matter is settled privately without a marshal ever having been contacted by the petitioner. These private negotiations/agreements between petitioner and respondent may take place at any time (before the marshal requests the warrant, before or after the marshal serves notice, after the marshal has scheduled an eviction…)

There was one marshal who was not using the program because according to the handbook, he had a low volume of eviction cases and he did not have to be computerized. However, the marshal is no longer doing evictions.

3. Relatedly, in the ‘Schedule Status’ column of the dataset, all ~38k observations are listed as ‘Scheduled’ (in the data dictionary the column is described as either having values ‘Scheduled’, ‘Pending’, or ‘Confirmed). Assuming this is a mistake, when can we expect an update to the data in this column?

​This ‘Scheduled Status’ field should read either “Pending,” meaning not yet scheduled, or “Scheduled” meaning it’s on the marshal’s calendar. This is the way it should appear on open data. The actual scheduled date and pending evictions are not for publication due to safety reasons. The CPR has a “Confirmed” field which is an automatic confirmatio …

tickets.question: If two records have the same court index number, address, unit number, date, and marshal, but different docket numbers, are they the same eviction? What do different docket numbers signify?
tickets.reply:
Thank you for inquiry.  Per the Data Dictionary associated with the Evictions dataset, the docket number is assigned by the City Marshal upon case intake. Upon receiving an eviction case, the City Marshal enters the information into their official electronic docket book which automatically assigns a unique docket number for each court-ordered judgment. Each warrant of eviction enforced at a location will have its own unique docket number. For example, if there are multiple tenants at a location there may be multiple court-ordered judgments. Different docket numbers under one court index number are based on how many judgements the court ordered on the case.

Thank you,
- NYC DOI Open Data

tickets.question:
Hello, 
I'm working on a data project on eviction data and have a few questions: 
1) According to the provided metadata, this dataset is updated daily. How often do NYC Marshals report these eviction cases? Are they reported immediately into this database? I would like to understand how complete the most recent entries are.
2) I noticed that a few entries have dates set in the future (up to 08.12.2025). Can these be attributed to data entry errors or are there other explanations?
Thank you so much for your time!
tickets.reply: The online dataset is updated daily and Marshals report data daily. Marshals enter data when they serve notices of eviction and when they schedule evictions, and evictions are generally scheduled the day before the eviction will take place. Therefore, the dataset generally has up-to-date information within a few days of a notice and/or eviction. Generally dates of eviction will not be set more than two weeks in the future so data outside of that range is more than likely an error. You can reach out to the individual Marshal for additional information. However, the date cited in the query is in the past (08.12.2025), not the future.

Hello there, 
My name is ***, and I am currently a 3rd year PhD student in ***. My question is: What does it mean when observations have the same court index number, docket number, and same address, but appears twice with two different executed dates? For example, please see court index number, ***. 
Intertwined with this question is, when observations have the same court index number, same address, and same executed dates, but different docket numbers, does that mean that multiple individuals were evicted from the same location?
Any help with the questions above would be greatly appreciated! Thank you so much!
tickets.reply: There may be multiple entries for the same index number in cases where separate warrants were requested to evict separate tenants (different docket number, same index) and there may be multiple entries per docket record in cases where warrants were executed twice. After eviction a tenant may go to court and obtain an “Order to Show Cause,” to be restored to possession of the premises under a stipulation, and if the tenant defaults on the stipulation the warrant can be re-executed. The New York State Courts Electronic Filing (NYSCEF) system may provide additional detail on records by index number, as long as the cases are on NYSCEF (pro-se cases are not required to be electronically filed). Good luck in your studies.

Original:

I see in the footnotes for the NYPD Complaint Historic dataset that complaints that occur in parks are geocoded to the nearest street intersection (rather than in the park itself). It appears that for most crimes, the field "PREM_TYP_DESC" indicates where the complaint happened (in a residence, on the street, in a park, etc.). tickets.reply:

Thank you for your interest in the NYPD Complaint dataset.
The records for murder/homicide are maintained separately from other complaints. As such, not all the same fields are tracked.  As you noted, one of these fields is the prem_typ_desc, which s why it is null for these rows.
Furthermore, since each complaint is anonymized geographically by moving the incident to the closest mid-block point, there is no way to determine exactly where an incident occurred.

Edit/Follow-up Response:
Thank you for your inquiry on the NYPD’s Complaint Historic Dataset, with a focus on the “murder & non-negligent manslaughter” charges occurring in and around Central Park. As previously inquired, the murders are tracked and recorded differently than other complaints make the some of the data fields such as “PREM_TYP_DESC” have null values.

In regards to murders occurring in or around Central Park, a dataset was pulled for the calendar years of 2020 and 2021 to review the actual locations of the murders. During those years, no murders were in Central Park. A way to verify this with open data dataset is to look at the field “ADDR_PCT_CD” which indicates the precinct of occurrence. In this case, the number 22 is used for the Central Park Precinct, which there are no murders for those years.

When it comes to see if a crime happened in a transit jurisdiction, the field “JURIS_DESC” with the value “N.Y. TRANSIT POLICE” would be used.

Thank you again for your inquiry.

tickets.question: I'd like more information about one of the variables. The codebook is a little thin on the matter. The variable is INITIAL_SEVERITY_LEVEL_CODE. how exactly are these assigned? They appear to be lower numbers are higher priorities, but this is not explicit. Is the same method used in all years, months, cases? etc. Ideally, I'd like to be put in touch with someone with intimate knowledge of this particular data set. Thank you!
tickets.reply:
When someone calls 9-1-1 and reaches an EMS Alarm Receipt Dispatcher (ARD), the ARD asks a number of questions to triage the call and determine its type and severity. This is determined through a computer algorithm that acts as a decision tree to find a call type through previous responses. Our EMS ARDs are also trained EMTs and they have the ability to override the computerized triage algorithm.

The call type determines which what type of resource the incident will receive. In our case, it will receive an Advanced Life Support (ALS) ambulance, a Basic Life Support (BLS) ambulance, a DUAL response (ALS+BLS) and in some cases a Certified First Responder (CFR) response. CFRs include all of our Fire Engine companies.

Each call type is mapped to a severity level. The severity level determines which incidents will get an unit assigned to the incident first. Severity levels 1-3 (also called segments) are categorized as life-threatening emergencies. 4-8 are non-life threatening emergencies. Note that not all of the highest priorities have the same type of response.

Each incident will have an initial and final severity level and call type because it can be important to know how the incident was originally triaged (based on the information the first caller gave) and how that categorization may have changed base on new information from additional callers or other trained personnel on scene or changes in patient condition, for example.

I hope this is helpful.

tickets.question:
There are some parts of the data dictionary that are not clear:
- How do I interpret INITIAL_SEVERITY_LEVEL_CODE and  FINAL_SEVERITY_LEVEL_CODE?
- The description for the incident disposition codes are not clear to me. For example I am unsure what 90 (unfounded) means or 95 (triaged at scene no transport). I am also unsure about the difference between 87 (cancelled) and CANCEL (cancelled). I have a few more uncertainties, but I was wondering if there is a way I can get a more detailed description for all incident disposition codes?

Thank you in advance!
tickets.reply:
1. INITIAL_SEVERITY_LEVEL_CODE & FINAL_SEVERITY_LEVEL_CODE
- Initial severity: This indicates the severity of the incident at the time it is first assigned, based on information provided by the caller (i.e., the first severity assigned to the incident).
- Final severity: This reflects the severity determined after the response and assessment by EMS personnel, likely when the incident is closed.
- Severity levels are generally ranked from 1 (most severe) to 8 (least severe), with 1–3 being life-threatening and 4–8 being non-life-threatening.
- Differences between initial and final severity may occur for a variety of reasons, such as additional phone calls or assessments conducted on scene.
2. Incident Disposition Codes
Disposition codes reflect the outcome or resolution of the incident. Examples include:
- 90 (Unfounded): No actionable incident was found after investigation.
- 95 (Triaged at scene, no transport): EMS evaluated the patient at the scene, but transport was not required.
- 87 (Cancelled) / “CANCEL”: The incident was cancelled before EMS arrival or transport. Both numeric and text codes typically indicate the same outcome, there is NO differences between the two.

tickets.question:
Questions about joining tables.  I would like to join the following tables:
1.  Can the datasets 'NYPD Calls for Service' and the 'EMS incident Dispatch Data' be joined?  if so, what is the joining field/key?
2.   Can the 'EMS incident Dispatch Data' and the 'NYPD use of Force' dataset be joined?  if so, what is the joining field/key?
Thanks in advance.
tickets.reply:
These datasets cannot be cleanly joined because the versions published on NYC Open Data contain limited fields and no shared incident ID between NYPD and EMS.
 
1. NYPD Calls for Service ↔ EMS Incident Dispatch
- No direct join key. NYPD and FDNY use separate CAD systems, and the Open Data versions don’t include any matching incident numbers.
- PD isn’t involved in every EMS incident, so even an approximate join won’t capture all overlap.
- Only possible join is fuzzy (date/time + location), and even that will be inconsistent due to limited fields.
 
2. EMS Incident Dispatch ↔ NYPD Use of Force
- No common identifier in the Open Data versions.
- Use-of-force events may or may not involve EMS, and EMS data on Open Data does not include NYPD incident numbers.
- Again, only approximate joins using time + location, but with low reliability.
 
Not all PD incidents involve EMS and vice versa; and even when they do, similar information available in both tables on Open Data is not a guaranteed incident match

tickets.question:
- Is there more information on the call type descriptions? For example, the difference between ARREST	and T-ARST is unclear as they have the same call type description. There are also some call types, such as MOSINJ and BPP, that are not in the data description.

- Is there more information on the severity level codes? For example, what is the difference between a 0 and a 9?

- Is there more information on the incident dispositions? For example, what is the difference between a patient pronounced dead and a patient gone on arrival?

- Is there more information on the dispatch area of the incident? For example, where exactly are M5 and K6? Also what is meant by dispatch area?
tickets.reply:
Question Asked:
- Is there more information on the call type descriptions? For example, the difference between ARREST and T-ARST is unclear as they have the same call type description. There are also some call types, such as MOSINJ and BPP, that are not in the data description.
Call Type Descriptions:
The Call Type field represents the nature of the incident as coded in the FDNY EMS Computer-Aided Dispatch (CAD) system.
- Codes with the “T-” prefix (e.g., ARREST vs T-ARST) indicate that the call information was electronically transmitted/texted into CAD rather than entered through the standard voice-based 911 intake process.
- The prefix reflects a different dispatch workflow only; the underlying medical complaint and public description remain the same.
- Some call types such as MOSINJ and BPP are internal CAD codes associated with severity level 9 and are typically related to incidents marked “Out of Service.” These records are not part of the public Open Data dataset and therefore are not included in the posted data description file.

Question Asked:
- Is there more information on the severity level codes? For example, what is the difference between a 0 and a 9?
Severity Level Codes:
Severity codes reflect the dispatcher’s triage-based assessment of urgency at the time of call intake.
- Severity levels are generally ranked from 1 (most severe) to 8 (least severe), with 1–3 being life-threatening and 4–8 being non-life-threatening.

Question Asked:
- Is there more information on the incident dispositions? For example, what is the difference between a patient pronounced dead and a patient gone on arrival?
Incident Dispositions:
The Disposition field reflects the final outcome of the EMS response.
- Patient Pronounced Dead: EMS personnel determined that the patient was deceased at the scene according to formal protocol.
- Patient Gone on Arrival: EMS units arrived at the scene, but the patient was not present (e.g., the patient left before EMS arrival or could not be located).
- These outcomes are operationally distinct and represent different response results within standard EMS reporting.

Question Asked:
- Is there more information on the dispatch area of the incident? For example, where exactly are M5 and K6? Also what is meant by dispatch area?
Dispatch Area:
Dispatch Area refers to the internal operational response zone responsible for assigning EMS resources—not a precise patient address. The letter identifies the borough (M = Manhattan, K = Brooklyn/Kings, Q = Queens, X = Bronx, S/R = Staten Island), and the number identifies a specific EMS sector within that borough (e.g., M5 = Manhattan Zone 5; K6 = Brooklyn Zone 6).
Exact geographic boundaries of these zones are not included in the public dataset to protect patient privacy. Detailed maps and boundary definitions are maintained in FDNY EMS internal documentation.

tickets.reply:

tickets.question: if your name shows up under the "civil service list certification" what does that mean? what the certification Expiration Date mean if we did not receive a notice and what will happen to your name on this list?
tickets.reply:
A List Certification includes the names of a group of eligible candidates on an established, active Civil Service Eligible List, and it is provided to an appointing agency by DCAS to fill available positions.  The number of names on a List Certification depends on the number of available positions being filled and the number of candidates on an eligible list with identical scores.

An agency may use a given List Certification for filling positions between the date that the Certification is created and the Certification Expiration Date.  If a candidate has not received a notice it means that the agency did not use the Certification or that the candidate was not reached for consideration of appointment.  If a candidate does not receive a notice in connection with a specific List Certification, the candidate’s name remains on the underlying Eligible List and would remain available for future certifications.

tickets.question: What action is completed for some applicants to have a list agency code / description and some do not? As well as the request date. Is this information updated once called for a hiring pool?
tickets.reply:
The "List Agency Code" column indicates whether the list certification pertains to an Open Competitive exam or a Promotional exam. If the value in the field is "000", the list certification pertains to an Open Competitive exam, where candidates may be called by any agency with openings in the title. If the value in the field is a three-digit agency code, the list certification pertains to a Promotional exam, where candidates may be called for promotional openings at the agency in which they are employed.

The "Request Date" column reflects the date on which an agency submits a request to DCAS for names of candidates on the list who are eligible for appointment to an open position or positions.

The information on the Civil Service List Certification dataset does not pertain to actions taken by individual agencies following a certification, such as calling applicants to a hiring pool.

Thank you,
- NYC Department of Citywide Administrative Services

NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question:
Hello NYC Parks / NYC Open Data team,

Following my message of October 8 (RiskRating values below 3), I have three more questions, about Forestry Tree Points (hn5i-inap) and Forestry Planting Spaces (82zj-84is).

1. Planting Spaces refresh. Planting Spaces (82zj-84is) lists an update frequency of "Every 2 weeks" with automation enabled, but its rows were last updated on 2025-03-05. Tree Points is refreshed every two weeks, so 26,888 current tree points now reference a planting space that is not in the published extract. Has the automated refresh of Planting Spaces stopped? Could it be restarted, or the stated frequency corrected?

2. TPStructure values. Could you publish the allowed values of TPStructure with their definitions (Full, Shaft, Stump, Stump - Uprooted, Retired)? In particular: is "Retired" always a removed tree (with a removal Work Order), and what is the structure of a tree after retirement? On Retired and Stump rows, do TPCondition, DBH and RiskRating show the tree's last state before retirement? (81,428 Retired and 38,142 Stump records carry a RiskRating.)

3. Permanent identifier. Of OBJECTID and GlobalID (the data dictionary marks both as Primary Key), which is guaranteed never to be reassigned or reused? And could a row identifier be set on Tree Points and Planting Spaces, as OBJECTID already is on Forestry Risk Assessments? Rows would then keep their identity across refreshes, and duplicate keys could not be published - Planting Spaces currently has 6,864 GlobalIDs that appear twice, identical on every column (for example 00005D02-BCEA-4814-8AA2-1C4696EB098B, OBJECTID 10930392).

Thank you,
***
tickets.reply:
Hi Nina,
Thanks for all of your questions about the ForMS (Forestry) datasets. I’ve included responses to all three of your inquiries (13107, 13111, 13120) in this email, and I’ve updated the data dictionary where possible, so feel free to take another look. Please see below and reach out if you need clarity on anything else.

1. re: Planting Spaces refresh. There was an error with our automation process. On 10/21, we pushed a manual update including data through 10/19. The automation script is being tweaked, but we plan to manually publish updates on the same monthly schedule.
2. re: TPStructure values. Retired means that the tree is no longer present. It may not necessarily have a removal work order. Regarding the Retired and Stump rows, yes, the DBH and RishRating show the tree’s last state before retirement.
3. re: Permanent identifier. ObjectIDs and, more reliably, GlobalIDs can usually be treated as persistent unique IDs that should last forever and never be re-used. Duplicates that appeared in error were removed by the most recent (10/21) data refresh.

tickets.question:
Hello NYC Parks / NYC Open Data team,

Following my messages of October 8 and 9 (tickets #13107 and #13111), I have five more questions, about Forestry Planting Spaces (82zj-84is), Forestry Tree Points (hn5i-inap) and Forestry Risk Assessments (259a-b6s7).

1. Duplicate planting spaces. Planting Spaces (82zj-84is) has 1,091,709 rows but only 1,084,845 distinct GlobalIDs: 6,864 GlobalIDs appear exactly twice, and each pair is identical on all 35 columns, OBJECTID included (for example GlobalID 00007383-6466-4C33-A715-3523186EEF66, OBJECTID 11041439). This follows question 3 of my message of October 9 on row identifiers. Is the duplication an artefact of the export, and will the copies be removed at the next refresh?
2. Implausible diameters. In Tree Points (hn5i-inap), 17 standing trees (TPStructure Full) have a DBH over 120 inches. Two examples: OBJECTID 1268531 (northern red oak, Quercus rubra) at 2,427 inches, and OBJECTID 2412695 (Chinese elm, Ulmus parvifolia) at 1,310 inches. Could you confirm or correct these values? Is there an accepted maximum, or a validation rule, for DBH in ForMS?
3. DBH of 0 and blank DBH. In Tree Points, DBH is 0 on 22,549 rows (644 of them standing trees, TPStructure Full) and blank on 24,840 rows (76 of them standing trees). Does 0 mean "not measured" or "not applicable", or is it a real measurement (for example a newly planted tree below measuring height)? Do 0 and blank mean different things? This is separate from my question 2 of October 9 about Retired and Stump rows.
4. Risk assessments on Sidewalk Rating inspections. The Risk Assessments (259a-b6s7) description says risk assessments are sub-components of inspections where Type = Level 2, but some are attached to "Sidewalk Rating" inspections. Two examples: objectid 184915 (inspection D3F9B780-63F8-4CFB-BD8F-F559180C4B9E, created 2018-03-06, "No Visible Defect", rating 3) and objectid 3477976 (inspection F152DC53-0B44-45D5-BFBB-C0F2D8561511, created 2021-03-10, "Root Problems", rating 3). Are risk assessments routinely scored during sidewalk inspections, and since when? Does Tree Points RiskRating take the most recent assessment from any inspection type, so that a sidewalk inspection's rating of 3 can replace an earlier Level 2 rating of 6 or 7, as on tree points 2496399 and 202797? If so, could the description be updated?
5. "DNP" in planting space status. In Planting Spaces (82zj-84is), PSStatus has the values "Empty - DNP" (1,690 spaces) and "Retired - DNP" (1,442 spaces), counted over distinct spaces. What does DNP stand for? Should an "Empty - DNP" space be counted as available planting capacity? The data dictionary entry for PSStatus (row 2.021) says only "Indicates if planting space is populated, empty, or retired"; could the values be listed with definitions?
Thank you,
***
tickets.reply:
Hi ****,
Thanks for all of your questions about the ForMS (Forestry) datasets. I’ve included responses to all three of your inquiries (13107, 13111, 13120) in this email, and I’ve updated the data dictionary where possible, so feel free to take another look. Please see below and reach out if you need clarity on anything else.

1. re: Duplicate planting spaces. Duplicates that appeared in error were removed by the 10/21 data refresh.
2. re: Implausible diameters. These values are attributed to manual data entry errors. There is no validation rule for DBH values in ForMS. While these trees can be put into a queue for re-inspection, we have no timeline as to when the values will be updated to correct the errors.
3. re: DBH of 0 and blank DBH. Generally speaking, zeros and blanks in the DBH field are likely for trees that originated as stumps, and had no DBH to measure. DBH is required field for Tree Points, but blanks and zeros are not part of the data validation for that field. These values for the standing trees are likely due to data entry errors. There is no validation rule for DBH values in ForMS.
4. re: Risk assessments on Sidewalk Rating inspections. Yes, Risk Assessments are a part of Sidewalk inspections, and the tree point takes the most recent risk rating from any inspection type that has a risk assessment (Level 2, Level 3, and Sidewalk Rating Inspection).
5. “DNP” in planting space status. DNP stands for “Do Not Plant” and is a designation used by a Forester to indicate this particular planting space is no longer viable for various reasons (utilities, underground vaults, etc.)

tickets.question:
Hi,
I would like to know of there is a way to link the forestry service request dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Environment/Forestry-Service-Requests/mu46-p9is) with the forestry work order dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Environment/Forestry-Work-Orders/bdjm-n7q4).
tickets.reply:
Hello,

Thank you for contacting NYC Parks regarding the Forestry datasets. To join Foresty Service Requests to Forestry Work Orders use the following keys:

1. Join Forestry Service Requests "GlobalID" to Forestry Inspections "ServiceRequestGlobalID"
2. Join Forestry Inspections "GlobalID" to Forestry Work Orders "InspectionGlobalID"

Keep in mind that a service request does not always result in a work order. Upon inspection, our staff determines what work is required.

The Forestry Management System user guide and dictionary provides all of the information from the data collection in one place.

Best,
NYC Parks and the NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question:
Good afternoon,

I have been reviewing these three NYC Parks datasets on NYC Open Data and was hoping to get some clarification on how they are created and managed:

Forestry Service Requests: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/mu46-p9is
Forestry Inspections: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/4pt5-3vv4
Forestry Work Orders: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/bdjm-n7q4

The published descriptions and ForMS user guide explain that these activities are recorded in the Forestry Management System. I’m trying to understand exactly how the public datasets relate to those underlying agency records.

1. Creation and updating: Are these three datasets direct exports from ForMS, or are they compiled through another process? Which Parks team creates and updates the public exports, and what role does the NYC Open Data team have? Are any records or fields transformed, combined or entered separately before publication?

2. Completeness: Does each public dataset contain every corresponding service request, inspection or work order in ForMS for its stated period, or only selected records or fields? If it is not complete, what is excluded and why? In particular, are there date limits, status filters, privacy exclusions, legacy-system limits or other criteria? I’m trying to distinguish withheld fields from omitted records, rather than assume that a public export is a complete copy of the internal system.

The Forestry Service Requests description states that requests created internally can lack a 311 number and do not appear in 311. Are all such internally created requests included in the Forestry Service Requests export? Similarly, are inspections initiated internally, including sidewalk-rating inspections, and their related work orders included in the public tables?

3. Relationship to records searches: When Parks responds to FOIL requests or conducts records searches for forestry conditions, inspections or repairs, are these public datasets searched, or are searches performed in ForMS or other internal systems? If the internal records are broader, what types of related material, such as inspection notes, photographs, correspondence or attachments, are not included in the public tables?

If another team manages these exports or can answer the records-search question, could you please forward the relevant portion or let me know whom to contact? Existing documentation explaining the export process and inclusion criteria would also be helpful.

Thank you for your help!
What is the coordinate system you used to map the tree points? I am working on a project, and this information would be very helpful! Thank you.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting the Open Data HelpDesk! We use the NY State Plane Coordinate System, NAD_1983_StatePlane_New_York_Long_Island_FIPS_3104_Feet. The ID is 2263.

Thank you,
NYC Department of Parks and Recreation (PARKS)

tickets.question:
Hello NYC Parks / NYC Open Data team,

I am working with Forestry Tree Points (hn5i-inap, data last updated October 7, 2026) and have a question about the RiskRating column.

Your data dictionary documents the Risk Assessments RiskRating as 3-12, "Combination of Failure, Impact Target, and Consequence" (each scored 1-4). In Forestry Tree Points, 72 rows carry a RiskRating below that range: 0 on 14 rows, 1 on 22 rows and 2 on 36 rows, with RiskRatingDate between 2017-02-24 and 2020-01-03. Examples (GlobalID, each rated 0, dated 2020-01-03): 154E6059-6C9A-403D-9048-1B9BF46DF6BD, 0B250E1A-801F-4843-A7A8-45BC9A0DD364, 090AE20D-95D5-4F76-8E73-9575A8377C7B.

My questions:
1. What do ratings of 0, 1 and 2 mean - a placeholder, an earlier scale, or a data-entry error? Should they be treated as missing?
2. When one Level 2 inspection records several defects (several Risk Assessment rows), which total does the tree point's RiskRating keep - the highest, or another rule?

In case it is useful: in Forestry Risk Assessments (259a-b6s7), RiskRating equals Failure + ImpactTarget + Consequence on 1,544,190 of the 1,544,207 rows that have all four values; 16 of the 17 exceptions have CreatedDate 2017-09-26.

Thank you,
***
tickets.reply:
Hi ****
Thanks for all of your questions about the ForMS (Forestry) datasets. I’ve included responses to all three of your inquiries (13107, 13111, 13120) in this email, and I’ve updated the data dictionary where possible, so feel free to take another look. Please see below and reach out if you need clarity on anything else.
1. RiskRatings of 0, 1, and 2 should be treated as missing, as they were due to bugs in a prior version of the ForMS database.
2. When one Level 2 inspection records several defects (several Risk Assessment rows), the tree point’s RiskRating keeps the highest value associated with the most recent inspection.
3. Regarding this note: [RiskRating equals Failure + ImpactTarget + Consequence on 1,544,190 of the 1,544,207 rows that have all four values; 16 of the 17 exceptions have CreatedDate 2017-09-26.] – This is likely due to bugs in the ForMS system when Risk Assessments and our Tree Risk Management inspection protocol was first being developed, tested and implemented in ForMS.

tickets.question: I am looking for open data with the date of new tree plantings by NYC Parks Forestry Unit. New trees that die within the first two years of plantings are under warranty by NYC Parks. I am looking for a data set with the date of new tree planting to for neighborhood volunteers to check on the tree health of these newly planted trees.
tickets.reply:
Thanks for your inquiry. 
To clarify, the guarantee period for newly planted trees is either 1 or 2 years, depending on the contract for a particular tree. 
For trees planted within the past year or two, on Open Data you can join Forestry Inspections (TreePointGlobalID) to Forestry Tree Points (GlobalID) to find a tree's PlantedDate (if known). PlantedDate is a field in the Forestry Tree Points dataset. The field had not been populated consistently prior to 2025. 

A more user-friendly option is the online Street Tree Planting tracker, which displays completed plantings from the past 6 months and plantings scheduled into 2027. There is a link to download the data as a CSV as well. This is part of the larger Parks Tree Work Hub. Hope this helps! 

Best,

NYC Parks
Open Data Team

For trees planted within the past year or two, on Open Data you can join Forestry Inspections (TreePointGlobalID) to Forestry Tree Points (GlobalID) to find a tree's PlantedDate (if known). NYC Parks

tickets.question:
Good afternoon,

I have been reviewing these three NYC Parks datasets on NYC Open Data and was hoping to get some clarification on how they are created and managed:

Forestry Service Requests: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/mu46-p9is
Forestry Inspections: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/4pt5-3vv4
Forestry Work Orders: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/d/bdjm-n7q4

The published descriptions and ForMS user guide explain that these activities are recorded in the Forestry Management System. I’m trying to understand exactly how the public datasets relate to those underlying agency records.

1. Creation and updating: Are these three datasets direct exports from ForMS, or are they compiled through another process? Which Parks team creates and updates the public exports, and what role does the NYC Open Data team have? Are any records or fields transformed, combined or entered separately before publication?

2. Completeness: Does each public dataset contain every corresponding service request, inspection or work order in ForMS for its stated period, or only selected records or fields? If it is not complete, what is excluded and why? In particular, are there date limits, status filters, privacy exclusions, legacy-system limits or other criteria? I’m trying to distinguish withheld fields from omitted records, rather than assume that a public export is a complete copy of the internal system.

The Forestry Service Requests description states that requests created internally can lack a 311 number and do not appear in 311. Are all such internally created requests included in the Forestry Service Requests export? Similarly, are inspections initiated internally, including sidewalk-rating inspections, and their related work orders included in the public tables?

3. Relationship to records searches: When Parks responds to FOIL requests or conducts records searches for forestry conditions, inspections or repairs, are these public datasets searched, or are searches performed in ForMS or other internal systems? If the internal records are broader, what types of related material, such as inspection notes, photographs, correspondence or attachments, are not included in the public tables?

If another team manages these exports or can answer the records-search question, could you please forward the relevant portion or let me know whom to contact? Existing documentation explaining the export process and inclusion criteria would also be helpful.

Thank you for your help!

Hi,
I would like to know of there is a way to link the forestry service request dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Environment/Forestry-Service-Requests/mu46-p9is) with the forestry work order dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Environment/Forestry-Work-Orders/bdjm-n7q4).
tickets.reply:
Hello,

Thank you for contacting NYC Parks regarding the Forestry datasets. To join Foresty Service Requests to Forestry Work Orders use the following keys:

1. Join Forestry Service Requests "GlobalID" to Forestry Inspections "ServiceRequestGlobalID"
2. Join Forestry Inspections "GlobalID" to Forestry Work Orders "InspectionGlobalID"

Keep in mind that a service request does not always result in a work order. Upon inspection, our staff determines what work is required.

The Forestry Management System user guide and dictionary provides all of the information from the data collection in one place.

Best,
NYC Parks and the NYC Open Data Team

The bike lane on Flushing Ave in Brooklyn Navy Yard area (bikeid: 4463, prevbikeid: 1171) has the wrong retired/installed date. According to Google street view, the curbside bike lane became a sidewalk level bike lane somewhere between July 2019 and November 2020, the current install date however is 6/2/2022. 

There are also numerous errors with the instdate column, with date going back to the early 1900s and 1930s, I'm certain that no bike lane was installed back then. 

Further, the current data dictionary also doesn't provide a definition on what counts as a greenway. All of these errors make it difficult for me to isolate protected bike lanes that were constructed by taking away road space, and when they were put in place.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your request, please see response from the Bike Unit: 
1. The bike lane on Flushing Ave in Brooklyn Navy Yard area (bikeid: 4463, prevbikeid: 1171) has the wrong retired/installed date. According to Google street view, the curbside bike lane became a sidewalk level bike lane somewhere between July 2019 and November 2020, the current install date however is 6/2/2022. 
- Bike infrastructure projects may take months or years to reach completion and may be functionally available to riders before the official installation date. We will review the portion of the bike network you identified for accuracy as we strive to improve the data.
1. There are also numerous errors with the instdate column, with date going back to the early 1900s and 1930s, I'm certain that no bike lane was installed back then. 
- New York City has an extensive history with bicycling and the first asphalt roads in Brooklyn were specifically paved for bicycle traffic in the 1800s! Multiple dedicated bicycle paths were first installed in the 1800s in New York and are still an important part of the bicycle network to this day. Accordingly, you will find bicycle facilities that date back through the 1800s and 1900s in the data.
1. Further, the current data dictionary also doesn't provide a definition on what counts as a greenway. All of these errors make it difficult for me to isolate protected bike lanes that were constructed by taking away road space, and when they were put in place.
- Please visit https://www.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/bicyclists/greenways.shtml for current information about NYC's Greenways program and maps of the network. Greenways are not a specific type of bicycle facility in New York; rather, they are designated corridors that play an important role in the bike network. Protected bike lanes and paths are a facility type that comprise much of the greenway network, and may repurpose part of or be installed in underutilized public rights-of-way.

tickets.question: We're trying to join this dataset with the DOB Job Application Filings dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/browse?q=DOB%20Job%20Application%20Filings&sortBy=relevance) to create a field called "C/O Issue Date." Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be a good field to join the datasets together as it looks like the C/O Dataset has a different Job # than the Job Filings dataset. Any tips for how to join these two together? Using geometry could be problematic because there may be multiple job filings at the same location over time.
tickets.reply:
Hi,

Job Number is the key that joins these two datasets together. I suspect that you are expecting the 2 datasets to match up neatly and not have any records left out on either side, which won't be the case.

The Job Applications dataset only includes job applications with a "Latest Action Date" since January 1, 2000. In addition to that, these applications are in every phase of the process from first submission to final Sign Off.

The Certificates of Occupancy (CO) dataset contains all COs issued since 7/12/12. Final COs are only issued after a job is signed off. A Temporary Certificate of Occupancy (TCO) may be issued earlier, but not every job will get a TCO. A CO can also be issued for older jobs that may not be in the other dataset.

Please review the Data Dictionaries for these datasets on their home pages in the Attachments section. If you want to get more information about a specific record, use our Building Information System (BIS). And if you still have specific questions about the data, feel free to come back here and ask me.

Thank you,
- , DOB Open Data Coordinator

Sign up for our Open Data mailing list here.

tickets.question: Hi, I'm checking certificate of occupancy status for Jackson Park, a multifamily development with 3 towers and 3 building IDs. https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/DOB-Certificate-Of-Occupancy/bs8b-p36w I can find the certificate of occupancy details for building ID 4596920 and 4596921. But I can't find the certificate of occupancy data for building ID 4618925. Why isn't certificate of occupancy data for 4618925 showing up when I download the certificate of occupancy data?
tickets.reply:
Hi ,

This is an unfortunate side effect of a known data problem with Department of Buildings (DOB) BINs. We are working to clean this up, but here's the explanation:

Sometimes when there is new construction, our BIN data gets out of sync with the master list of BINs set by Department of City Planning (DCP). Due to issues surrounding the business process of getting permits for a new building, the building's records might be related to a "Dummy" BIN, which has an 8 as the second digit. These Dummy BINs will not show up in any other agency's data.

In this particular case, you can see on our BIS system that BIN 4618925 (http://a810-bisweb.nyc.gov/bisweb/PropertyProfileOverviewServlet?bin=4618925&go4=+GO+&requestid=0) has 2 other Dummy BINs associated with it (Additional BINs for Building). The current Certificate of Occupancy is actually tied to BIN 4856065 (http://a810-bisweb.nyc.gov/bisweb/PropertyProfileOverviewServlet?requestid=9&bin=4856065). And if you use that BIN on our Certificates of Occupancy dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/DOB-Certificate-Of-Occupancy/bs8b-p36w/data), you'll see the recent history of COs there.

Another way to disentangle this issue is to look at the Borough, Block and Lot. Those may match when the BIN doesn't.

So if you're looking at the Buliding Footprints dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/Building-Footprints/nqwf-w8eh), and you can't find a matching record in DOB data, this is likely the reason why. We are working closely with DCP to fix this problem.

Thank you,
- DOB Open Data Coordinator

Hello,

I am interested in this dataset on traffic speeds for a research project I am conducting at the Computer Science Department at *****. Specifically, I am interested in gaining further understanding of the different columns of this dataset, and what the speed and travel_time columns represent - I looked in the metadata but still have questions about the length of the interval that each speed is calculated for, what the ID variables represent, and how many different sensors there are, among other questions.

*****
tickets.reply:
Apologies for the delay and thank you for your request with New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT). Additional information as follows:
- Data are captured and retained every one minute. 
- Each link_point, one set of Lat, Long coordinates (40.7714206, -73.83345), is a sensor. 
- The “speed” column captures the average travel speed in miles per hour between the beginning (first set of Lat, Long coordinates) and end (last set of Lat, Long coordinates) of “link_points”. 
- The “travel_time” represents the average travel time in seconds between the beginning and end of “link_points”. 
- There are link points between stretches to capture additional speed information and travel time (number of seconds between each link_points) used to calculate average speed and travel time. 
- The ID is associated with the Link_Name (location of the stretch). 
- 453 locations speeds have been captured, but there could be locations that have since retired.
We will update the metadata to include this additional information.
Visit NYC DOT Real Time Traffic Conditions and Cameras for more information. If you have any additional questions, feel free to reply to this email or contact NYC DOT via webform- choose topic Traffic Congestion . 
 Thank you,
Best, 
 Department of Transportation (DOT)

tickets.question: How are parking violations for FY 2022 published already? I see that most of the data is for June and July 2022. Where can I find data for tickets that were issued in 2021?
tickets.reply:
There are two separate datasets that are published to Open Data; the Fiscal Year Issuance file and the Open Parking and Camera Violations dataset.

The Fiscal Year issuance dataset is updated once a month on the sixteenth with the prior month's new issuance.
Use the FY2021 issuance dataset and search for speed camera violations in each month.
Parking Violations Issue Fiscal Year 2021: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Parking-Violations-Issued-Fiscal-Year-2021/pvqr-7yc4

The Open Parking and Camera Violations dataset is updated daily with status updates to existing violations in the dataset, new violations are added to the dataset on Sundays. A data set uploaded on Sunday will have data for up to the Thursday of that week which just ended.

To search for issuance in a specific month, use the referenced data set because the Open Parking and Camera dataset doesn’t support date range searches.

Open Parking and Camera Violation: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Open-Parking-and-Camera-Violations/nc67-uf89





Thank you,
NYC DOF

https://idognames.com/top/methodology

tickets.reply: As described in the dataset descriptions and the data dictionary, the Dog Licensing dataset contains active dog licenses, and each record is a unique dog license period and not a unique dog. We will consider adding information to this dataset that allows users to identify unique dogs licensed.

tickets.agency: Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
tickets.question:
1. What was the lower limit of detection for arsenic, lead, and mercury?
2. the description says "Certain consumer products are also tested for other metals such as arsenic and mercury." How was it decided to test for other metals?
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your inquiries! We believe that these are the answers you are looking for:

What was the lower limit of detection for arsenic, lead, and mercury?
If you are asking about the amount of metal found in the sample of product tested under the "concentration" column, a sample with a metal concentration of "-1" means that there is no detection of metal concentration.

The description says, "certain consumer products are also tested for other metals such as arsenic and mercury". How was it decided to test for other metals?
This is collected as part of the DOHMH surveillance activities and entered into an internal Health Department application called Non-Paint Samples Datastore (NPSD). The metal concentrations of those tested products are then uploaded into NPSD. It's also being used by national and international public health authorities, such as poisoning prevention programs and non-governmental organizations (NGO's) to learn about potential hazardous consumer products associated with poisonings. This data has also triggered broader actions (see https://www.nature.com/articles/s41370-023-00525-1... The surveillance data also informs risk communication messaging (see www.nyc.gov/hazardousproducts)

Thank you,
DOHMH Open Data Team

tickets.question:
Hi - I had a few quick questions - thank you so much!!!
1. Do you have any information on the age of each cooling tower that is registered. 
2. Exactly what does "sample sates mean" - is that required water sampling? 
3. Are there any end markets that this dataset excludes? (e.g., healthcare, warehouses)

tickets.reply:
Our stewards responsible for this dataset were able to answer the questions below:
1. Do you have any information on the age of each cooling tower that is registered.
    a. A date of commissioning can be self-reported during registration for each piece of cooling tower equipment, but it is an optional field and it is not validated and thus not reported in OpenData. Date of commissioning is the date that the system was filled with water and started up (turned on).
2. Exactly what does "sample sates mean" - is that required water sampling?
    a. See the Data Dictionary’s column description for "Sample_Dates".
3. Are there any end markets that this dataset excludes? (e.g., healthcare, warehouses)
    a. This dataset contains cooling tower systems currently registered in the NYC Cooling Tower Registration Portal. You can review the requirements for registration in Local Law 77 of 2015. If we understand your question, you can see that the requirements for registration do not depend on the end market.
4. Is there any other data we can get on this from you guys?
    a. Results of Cooling Tower inspections conducted by the NYC Health Department can be found here and in Open Data here.
5. Does active equipment mean the number of cooling towers that building has?
    a. See the Data Dictionary’s column description for "Active_Equip"

tickets.question: Is there an indicator for when the park was opened? How is the "TYPECATEGO" and "SUBCATEGOR" determined? What do the variables "PERMIT" and "PIP_RATABL" indicate?
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting NYC Parks regarding the Parks Properties dataset.

Park Opening: The ACQUISITIONDATE is the best date to use for when a park "opened". This date indicates when the agency acquired the property. The date is not the easiest to read on the Open Data Portal but if you ignore the zeros the date appears.  For example, 19340803000000.00000 is 08/03/1934.

TYPECATEGORY: This field describes the type of property as defined by our Planning division at NYC Parks. There is a detailed list of type categories in the data dictionary (4th tab, titled "Typecategory").

SUBCATEGORY: This field defines the property as well, but the category is used by our Operations and Management Planning division (OMP). OMP is responsible for the Parks Inspection Program (PIP). You can learn more about the program here.

PIP_RATABLE: This field indicates if the property is rated as part of the Parks Inspection Program.

PERMIT: This field indicates if the property is available for reservation by permit, such as for a special event.

Thank you,
-NYC Parks and the NYC Open Data Team
