tickets.question:
On the recommendation of ***, I'm sending these questions here. I'd be extremely grateful for an opportunity to briefly interview the person managing the pension investment fund datasets:

1. While Period End Date specifies the end of the particular fiscal year, how can we determine at what date the decision to make a certain investment was made? 
2. What does Maturity Date specify? Is this when the investment being made starts to give returns? What is the timeline for when the returns from the respective investment also cease? Is this the date when the investment stopped earning interest? 
3. There is another date column in the dataset called  Date_as_of, what does that specify? The data dictionary has no explanation for this column.
4. From the dataset definitions, I understand that Original Face is the value of the investment when it was made, and the Base Total Cost is the amount of money the city had to pay out of pocket to buy the investments at original face value. Is this correct? If not, please explain the relationship between these two columns.
5. From the dataset definitions, I understand that Base Market Value specifies what the investment was worth in the market on the last day of the fiscal year. Which column of data specifies the exact amount of returns the pension fund received on the respective investment based on the decision to sell the asset? In addition, what is the best way of calculating how long the fund decided to hold certain investments and the one it has continued to hold for a long time (like more than a decade)? 
6. From the dataset definitions, I understand the Base Unrealized Gain/Loss, is calculated taking the Base Market Value (what it is worth now) and subtracting the Base Total Cost. But this would only indicate the "on paper" loss or gain from that investment. What would be the best method to determine the actual profitability of a certain investment?
tickets.reply:
Please find our response below:
 
1. While Period End Date specifies the end of the particular fiscal year, how can we determine at what date the decision to make a certain investment was made?
- Those data are not available in this dataset.
 
2. What does Maturity Date specify? Is this when the investment being made starts to give returns? What is the timeline for when the returns from the respective investment also cease? Is this the date when the investment stopped earning interest?
- A maturity date is the date on which a financial instrument reaches the end of its contractual life. At maturity, the obligations specified in the contract are settled, such as the repayment of principal, the final payment, or the completion of any remaining contractual commitments. For fixed income investments, the maturity date generally marks when the issuer repays the principal (or face value) to the investor and makes any final scheduled interest payment, after which the security ceases to exist. At maturity date, all gains and losses incurred by an investment during the holding are fully realized and, for interest-bearing instruments, interest no longer accrues. For other instruments, the maturity date is the date on which the contract expires or is settled according to its terms. Depending on the type of instrument, settlement may involve a cash payment, physical delivery of an underlying asset, or termination of the contract with no further obligations. 

3. There is another date column in the dataset called Date_as_of, what does that specify? The data dictionary has no explanation for this column.
- The “Data As Of” field in the file denotes the date at which the file was populated from the database. This is more of a version control tag: changes to any holdings attribute that occur between the Period End Date and the Data As Of date would be incorporated in this file.   

4. From the dataset definitions, I understand that Original Face is the value of the investment when it was made, and the Base Total Cost is the amount of money the city had to pay out of pocket to buy the investments at original face value. Is this correct? If not, please explain the relationship between these two columns.
- Original face amounts are fields populated specifically for pass-through securities. A unique feature of pass-through securities is that coupon payments include both principal and interest components. Hence, the underlying principal outstanding for the security declines over time. The original face is the original principal amount of a pass-through security at the time it is issued, before any principal has been repaid. It serves as the baseline against which future principal repayments and the remaining outstanding balance (shown in the Shares/Par Value field) are measured. The Base Total Cost field represents the total amount of money the investor paid for the instrument as of the Period End Date. These portfolios utilize an average costing method that takes into account all historical lots of a given position. In addition, the cost amount for fixed income securities may be adjusted for amortization/ accretion of discounts/premiums and for principal paydown activity on pass-through securities.

5. From the dataset definitions, I understand that Base Market Value specifies what the investment was worth in the market on the last day of the fiscal year. Which column of data specifies the exact amount of returns the pension fund received on the respective investment based on the decision to sell the asset? In addition, what is the best way of calculating how long the fund decided to hold certain investments and the one it has continued to hold for a long time (like more than a decade)?
- Base Market Value represents the amount an investor would expect to receive were they to liquidate the position in an orderly manner at the market close of the Period End Date. This amount is expressed in the portfolios’ base currency, USD. There are no fields av …

tickets.question:
When I download the data as a CVS I retrieve more than 2300  records. But when I download as an API only the first 1000 are retrieved.
Is there a parameter that I need to set or reset?
Thank you
tickets.reply:
I'm Aryanna from the NYC Open Data Team, nice to meet you! By default, the API returns a maximum of 1,000 records per request. To retrieve more than that, you can use the following techniques:
1. Increase the Limit: You can increase the number of records returned by using the $limit parameter. For example, to request 50,000 records:  https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/abcd-1234.json?$limit=50000
2. Paginate Using $offset: To request additional records, pair $limit with $offset to paginate through the data. This will allow you to pull the data in chunks:
    a. First Page: ?$limit=50000&$offset=0  
    b. Second Page: ?$limit=50000&$offset=50000  	
3. Optimize Your Query: Before making large requests, it's helpful to filter your results using the $select, $where, and $order parameters. This reduces unnecessary records and improves query performance.  
For more information on query parameters and how to work with large datasets please consult the following articles:  
- The LIMIT Clause documentation (https://dev.socrata.com/docs/queries/limit.html)
- How to Query More Than 1000 Rows (https://support.socrata.com/hc/en-us/articles/202949268-How-to-query-more-than-1000-rows-of-a-dataset)

tickets.reply:
Thanks for your inquiry! These are not errors. Records without a location are not actually for street work. They reflect payments, receipts, waivers, and other special cases. They are in this dataset because they are tracked in the same database that issues permits.


Example 1: Requests to do work during an embargo period require payment of a "MISCELLANEOUS - EMBARGO WAIVER REQUEST" fee before DOT will consider the request. This record reflects a payment rather than a location; associated permits issued after payment of the fee can be found by joining on the FullApplicationNo column.


Example 2: Some Oversized Vehicle permits are in the dataset. They used to be tracked in the same computer system as street work permits to allow trucks larger than the usual limit to travel on City streets.

Please let us know if you have further questions.


Thank you,
- NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question:
1. The BIC data dictionary and the dataset field name "TYPE OF VIOLATION" may be misleading. I suggest renaming it to "Adjudicating Agency."

2. I want to understand why different "FINE AMOUNT" values are allocated to respondents even though the "RULE CODE" violated is the same and the number of times the rule was violated is similar. For example:

3. How does early settlement affect the "FINE AMOUNT"?
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting the NYC Open Data Helpdesk! 
Reply to question 1: "TYPE OF VIOLATION” - that data point label indicates the court handling the violation (OATH) and is consistent with the one in our internal system. The field is defined in the data dictionary.


Reply to question 2: There are multiple factors that would allow for different “FINE AMOUNT” values.

- A company may choose to pay the violation in full when they receive it.
- A company may accept an early settlement offer to settle the violation without going through OATH.
- A company may provide mitigating factors to the Commission which may result in a different fine amount. For example, the penalty schedule allows for mitigating factors of certain violations to be considered.

Reply to question 3: An early settlement offer may lower the “FINE AMONT” a company is obligated to pay.


Thank you,
NYC Business Integrity Commission (BIC)

tickets.reply:
When trying to filter a dataset, there a couple of options you have. The open data portal allows you to use data in "grid" view or "explore" view. Grid view allows for basic filtering, sorting, etc. Explore view offers the same functionality as grid view, but with a more dynamic interface. To view any dataset on the portal in grid view, add "/data" to the end of its url. For example, this dataset's grid view url is: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/J-51-Exemption-and-Abatement/y7az-s7wc/data. To view any dataset in explore view, add "/explore" to the end of its url. For more help in filtering datasets, please refer to this guide and these videos. Hope this helps!

Thank you,
NYC Open Data Team

It looks like from your records that it went into effect in 2002, and should last for 14 years, which would have been 2016, but records stop at  2011. Can you please clarify?
tickets.reply:
The J51 benefit consists of both an exemption and an abatement. The abatement is provided upon the issuance of an HPD-approved Certificate of Eligibility (COE), and it can last for up to 20 years or until the abatement pool is depleted, whichever occurs first.

In the case below the lifetime abatement pool is $11, 250 and the abatement pool was depleted in TY12/13 as denoted in the breakdown below. Basically, there is a 20-year time limit to exhaust the abatement pool, but it generally depletes around 12 years.

tickets.question:
I've filtered the data by year for 2017-2021, looking at the number of records (buildings) returned and summing the number of units. Leaving aside the first pandemic year, 2017-19 are relatively stable:

2017 4,228 bldgs, 373,642 units
2018 4,571 bldgs, 385,420 units
2019 4,504 bldgs, 381,142 units

Compare 2021:

2021 5,007 bldgs, 440,823

We know that big bump does not reflect new buildings or new units, so how should I understand yearly variation in general, and how to interpret the big 2021 bump in particular?

>> Who would be best to speak to on this?

Thank you!
tickets.reply:
DOF trended the first pandemic year-FY21 (which is 2020 in the question) and did not run comp rent that year. COOP income and Expense were trended based on guideline trends and that year’s coop comp file was generated using the same logic. For FY21, the previous year’s comp files was used and the non-filers were removed. Last year, DOF valued post tentative roll and almost all coops were comp valued. As a result, the counts are much higher.

Thank you,
NYC Department of Finance (DOF)

tickets.question:
We pull "Dwelling Units" from the Bedbug Reporting data set. What fields can we pull Class A and Class B units, as presented at the top of HPD Online?
We currently pull "Dwelling Units" from this data set:
https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/Bedbug-Reporting/wz6d-d3jb
What fields in NYC Open Data will allow us to pull "A Units" and "B Units" for an address?

For example:
39 East 29 Street, Manhattan:
HPD online:
Top of page-142 A Units, 0 B Units
Bed Bugs section - 1,420 dwelling units (I believe this was a typo, with someone wanting to type in 142 units and 0 bed bugs in two different boxes, but ended up typing in "1 4 2 0" in a single box)
We are trying to get the correct number of apartments or units for an address. So if we can also pull the class A and class B units, as presented in HPD Online, we can correct typos in the "Dwelling units" field from Bedbug reporting.
Thanks!
tickets.reply:
The number of A units and B units can be found through the Buildings Subject to HPD Jurisdiction dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/Buildings-Subject-to-HPD-Jurisdiction/kj4p-ruqc). Each building in the Bedbug Reporting dataset (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/Bedbug-Reporting/wz6d-d3jb) has a unique ID which you can find on the first column of the Bedbug Reporting dataset. Using this unique Building ID, look up the specific building in the Buildings Subject to HPD Jurisdiction dataset. You should be able to find the number of "A Units" and "B Units" in the LegalClassA column and LegalClassB column.  Hope this helps!

Thank you,
- NYC HPD Open Data

Infested Dwelling Unit Count: The number of units, as reported by a tenant or otherwise known to the property owner, to have had a bedbug infestation during the reporting period. 
Eradicated Dwelling Unit Count: The number of units where eradication measures were employed during the reporting period.

The Government Publications Portal is one of the most useful civic tools. It has more than 78,000 agency reports in one searchable place,  and we lean on it all the time. The attached notes have the counts and what we found in DORIS's public code.

tickets.question:
Hello,

I'm looking for all the parking tickets given out for blocked bike lanes in fiscal year 2020. I see there are two datasets that may contain this data:

1. "Parking Violations Issued - Fiscal Year 2020" (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Parking-Violations-Issued-Fiscal-Year-2020/p7t3-5i9s)

2. "Open Parking and Camera Violations" (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Open-Parking-and-Camera-Violations/nc67-uf89)

Will all of the blocked bike lane tickets issued in FY20 appear in the first dataset? Or are there some that may appear only in the second dataset but not in the first?

Thanks,
*****
*****
*****
tickets.reply:
There are two separate datasets that are published to Open Data; the Fiscal Year Issuance file and the Open Parking and Camera Violations dataset.

The Fiscal Year issuance dataset is updated once a month on the sixteenth with the prior month's new issuance.
Use the FY2020 issuance dataset and search for speed camera violations in each month.
Parking Violations Issue Fiscal Year 2020: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Parking-Violations-Issued-Fiscal-Year-2020/pvqr-7yc4

The Open Parking and Camera Violations dataset is updated daily with status updates to existing violations in the dataset, new violations are added to the dataset on Sundays. A data set uploaded on Sunday will have data for up to the Thursday of that week which just ended.

To search for issuance in a specific month, use the referenced data set because the Open Parking and Camera dataset doesn’t support date range searches.

Open Parking and Camera Violation: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Open-Parking-and-Camera-Violations/nc67-uf89

Thank you,
- NYC DOF

tickets.question:
Hi, I would like to use NYPD call for service data to do analysis. Here I have some questions in understanding the dataset:

1. Why do some accidents have the same DISP_TS and ARRVD_TS? Does that mean the event does not need police to arrive at the scene?

1. Why do some accidents have ARRVD_TS = NA? Does that mean the recording is missing, or the event is not urgent that the police do not need to go?

tickets.reply:
In response to your specific questions:
1) if an incident has the same DISP_TS and ARRVD_TS that indicates that the member of service was on-scene when the incident was reported.  Typically this means that the member of service alerted dispatch to the incident rather than a member of the public.
2) Not all jobs require an ARRVD_TS.  Typical these are non critical or not serious incidents.

Thank you,
- NYPD Open Data Team

Questions about joining tables.  I would like to join the following tables:
1.  Can the datasets 'NYPD Calls for Service' and the 'EMS incident Dispatch Data' be joined?  if so, what is the joining field/key?
2.   Can the 'EMS incident Dispatch Data' and the 'NYPD use of Force' dataset be joined?  if so, what is the joining field/key?
Thanks in advance.
tickets.reply:
These datasets cannot be cleanly joined because the versions published on NYC Open Data contain limited fields and no shared incident ID between NYPD and EMS.
 
1. NYPD Calls for Service ↔ EMS Incident Dispatch
- No direct join key. NYPD and FDNY use separate CAD systems, and the Open Data versions don’t include any matching incident numbers.
- PD isn’t involved in every EMS incident, so even an approximate join won’t capture all overlap.
- Only possible join is fuzzy (date/time + location), and even that will be inconsistent due to limited fields.
 
2. EMS Incident Dispatch ↔ NYPD Use of Force
- No common identifier in the Open Data versions.
- Use-of-force events may or may not involve EMS, and EMS data on Open Data does not include NYPD incident numbers.
- Again, only approximate joins using time + location, but with low reliability.
 
Not all PD incidents involve EMS and vice versa; and even when they do, similar information available in both tables on Open Data is not a guaranteed incident match

tickets.question:
Hey guys, can you please tell me what kind of coordinates are being used for sign_x_coordinate and sign_y_coordinate?

We were hoping they would be longitudinal and latitudinal coordinates so we can could plot them on a map, but they don't seem to be? We're unclear what format they're in. If you can help me understand that, we might be able to convert them back to something we can use.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your inquiry. Unfortunately, the Street Sign Work Orders data does not include latitude (lat) and longitude (long) information, only X,Y. Alternatively New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) maintains a website for all New York City Parking Regulation Signs mapped, please visit: https://nycdotsigns.net/, the data is exportable to GeoJson. You may also use Geographic Information System (GIS) applications such as ESRI ArcGIS or the free open-source platform QGIS to perform conversions to Lat, Long, some basic application knowledge is required, see information below:

1) Using ArcGIS- license required
Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table. More information about the tool on the ArcGIS website:https://desktop.arcgis.com/en/arcmap/latest/manage...
ESRI community forum (https://community.esri.com/t5/arcgis-api-for-flex-questions/how-to-convert-x-y-to-lat-long/td-p/353854).
To do:
1. Load the data into the application as a CSV, add new columns in the attribute table (long and lat).
2. Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table (right click on the column header) to process the conversion. Fill in as follows:
a. Coordinates system of the data sources: NAD1983 State Plane New York Long Island FIPS 3104 Feet
b. Use coordinate system of the data frame: WGS 1984
c. Units: Decimal Degree

2) Using QGIS- free to download
More information from this blog: https://www.gisoutlook.com/2020/05/coordinate-conv...

To do:
1. Import CSV file: Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Delaminated Text Layer (CSV file)-> (keep everything else as default) only change Geometry CRS: EPSG:2263- NAD83/ New York Long Island (ftUS) -> add
2. Export layer+ Conversion: Export-> Save Feature As-> File Name: (select where to save the new file) Fill in as follows:
3. a. Format: CSV
4. b. CRS: EPSG:4326- WGS 84
5. c. Geometry: AS_XY
6.

Thank you,
NYC Department of Transportation, NYC Open Data Team

tickets.question: Is the commercial layer portion of this geodatabase the same as the Commercial District one represented in ZOLA? It looks different. The one in ZOLA appears as broader shapes than the one in the geodatabase. Are these different data or the same data just represented differently? tickets.reply:
We received your inquiry from the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. Our response is as follows: 
There our two layers in Zola that involve commercial zoning:
1. Commercial districts – these are areas zoned for commercial use and can be found under the Zoning Districts section in the Zola layers pane. These are a subset of records in the Zoning District layer within our NYC GIS Zoning Features dataset. You would filter for all districts that start with C in the ‘ZONEDIST’ field.
2. Commercial Overlay districts - commercial overlays districts are only C1-1 through C1-5 and C2-1 through C2-5 districts that mapped within residence districts. They tend to be mapped along streets that serve local retail needs and are found extensively throughout the city's lower- and medium-density areas and occasionally in higher-density districts. These are its own layer called Commercial Overlay District within our NYC GIS Zoning Features dataset. 
We hope this explains the difference between Commercial Districts and Commercial Overlay Districts, and which layers can be found in Zola and within our NYC GIS Zoning Features dataset.

tickets.question: I'm trying to connect the PAD and PLUTO files using the BBL identifier. There are examples where the same building has different BBL codes in the two files. One example is 200 North End Avenue, which is BBL 1000164601 in pad and 1000167520 in pluto
tickets.reply:
This could be an issue related to the version of PAD and PLUTO you are using. Please confirm you are using the latest version of each:
PAD = 18D
PLUTO = 18v1.1

I looked up 200 North End Avenue in GOAT and it confirms the BBL is 1000167520.

Both BBLs are technically correct, they are just at different levels. This BBL indicates that the building is a Condo. With Condos, the complex receives a lot number in the 7500 range, and each individual condo unit receives a condo unit lot number (1001-6999). So on Block 16 in Manhattan, condo unit lot number 4601 is a unit inside condo complex lot number 7520. PLUTO always assigns the condo complex lot number, unless it does not exist yet - then it would list the condo unit lot number.

You can also confirm this by checking Department of Finance (DOF) Digital Tax Map (DTM) application by entering either BBL.


Thank you,
- NYC Department of City Planning

tickets.question:
I am reporting a critical database indexing and synchronization error within the Property Address Directory (PAD) dataset regarding a condominium 1313-1323 Ave X built in 2005 located in Brooklyn, specifically identified as Tax Block 7398, Lot 1205 .
The Error Found:
The underlying Geosupport/PAD spatial data fails to synchronize with the static, legally approved condominium maps and Certificates of Occupancy on file with the City of New York. The physical layout of this condominium complex features 4 separate street addresses and 4 distinct Building Identification Numbers (BINs) existing under a single unified tax lot structure.
Due to a manual data entry or transcription error during the initial digitization of this multi-BIN complex, the accessory addresses and individual BINs are completely unlinked from the master building attributes on the city’s live geographic base maps. While the approved building plans explicitly authorize 8 legal parking spaces (split across the Certificates of Occupancy for the individual BINs, including 7 spaces linked to BIN 3378444 and 1 space linked to BIN 3378441), the dynamic mapping system queried by NYC Department of Buildings (DOB) enforcement inspectors defaults to showing a blank layout or a generic summary indicating only 2 spaces.

tickets.question:
Hello, I have a question about the specific indication of individual buildings in New York City LL87 Energy Audit Data. I am trying to find for each individual building in this dataset, what is its annual cooling energy use? I am referring to the "Existing Annual Energy Use_Electricity_space cooling" column for this information. My question though is concerning the "BINs" column indicating the specific building described by each row in the dataset. I am confused about how to handle entries in this column that list multiple BIN IDs, separated by semicolons. How should I treat these? Does this mean that all of the audit data for that particular row applies equally to all BIN IDs (individual buildings) listed in the "BINs" column for that row? For understanding the annual cooling energy use for that row, how does this value get distributed across all of the listed BIN IDs for that row? If I have multiple BIN IDs listed for that row, then how do I know how much of that annual cooling energy consumption value for that row was used by each of the buildings listed for that row? I would rely on New York City LL84 Energy Benchmarking Data, but from my understanding this dataset only includes whole building energy use intensity (EUI), which would not help me understand specific end use energy consumption, specifically whole building space cooling energy consumption. Is this correct, or should I be looking at another column here? I would appreciate any help in understanding how I could leverage NYC OpenData building energy consumption data to know how I can understand the cooling energy use of individual buildings.

Thank you for your time
tickets.reply: Our understanding is that LL87 is reported by BBL. BBLs may contain only a single building or multiple buildings, denoted by BINs. If it contains only a single building (single BIN #), then there will be only one Energy Efficiency Report (EER) submission for that BBL. If there are multiple buildings (multiple BINs) for the BBL and they all share the same base building systems then there will still only be one EER for that BBL, and all energy data applies to all buildings comprehensively. If there are multiple buildings but they each have their own base building systems then a separate EER will need to be submitted for each building (each BIN) and the energy data reported applies only to the individual building (individual BIN). Base building systems include: the building envelope, HVAC (Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning) systems, conveying systems, domestic hot water systems, and electrical and lighting systems.

tickets.question: The "wktgeom" column it gives coordinates. What is the "Coordinate Reference System" for these points?(i.e. epsg:4269)
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your inquiry. The Automated Traffic Volume Counts dataset contains X,Y coordinates. You may also search mapping WktGeom or convert the coordinates from X,Y to Lat, Long using Geographic Information System (GIS) applications. Examples of GIS applications are ESRI ArcGIS or the free open-source platform QGIS, some basic application knowledge is required, see options below:

1) Using ArcGIS- license required
Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table. More information about the tool on the ArcGIS website:https://desktop.arcgis.com/en/arcmap/latest/manage...
ESRI community forum (https://community.esri.com/t5/arcgis-api-for-flex-questions/how-to-convert-x-y-to-lat-long/td-p/353854).
To do:
1. Export data to CSV and format the WktGeom column (remove "POINT" and parentheses). Separate the X,Y into two columns (use the space as the break.)
2. Load the data into the application as a CSV, add new columns in the attribute table (long and lat).
3. Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table (right click on the column header) to process the conversion. Fill in as follows:
a. Coordinates system of the data sources: NAD1983 State Plane New York Long Island FIPS 3104 Feet
b. Use coordinate system of the data frame: WGS 1984
c. Units: Decimal Degree

2) Using QGIS- free to download
More information from this blog: https://www.gisoutlook.com/2020/05/coordinate-conv...

To do:
1. Import CSV file: Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Delaminated Text Layer (CSV file)-> (keep everything else as default) only change Geometry CRS: EPSG:2263- NAD83/ New York Long Island (ftUS) -> add
2. Export layer+ Conversion: Export-> Save Feature As-> File Name: (select where to save the new file) Fill in as follows:
3. a. Format: CSV
4. b. CRS: EPSG:4326- WGS 84
5. c. Geometry: AS_XY

Thank you,
NYC Department of Transportation, NYC Open Data Team

Last March I sent a request through this form asking for this data to be updated as it had been dormant since December 2022 (Inquiry ID #10761). In Queens alone, for the year 2020, there are records for 90 unique streets in the old dataset, but only 10 unique streets in the new dataset, despite supposedly having 1 year's worth of new data, in addition to previously recorded data.

This is just one example of a discrepancy between the two sets. Due to the large volume of data we could not narrow down the exact differences between both versions. But, since this is a widely-used and critical dataset for transit researchers, I wanted to reach out and ask if anyone is aware of this issue, and to hopefully see a fix or explanation come in the future. What is the logic for the sign codes in the signs.csv file (eg PS-65C, SP-477B, etc)? Do you have a guide/legend to help decipher what Sign Description the codes represent?
tickets.reply:
Greetings,

The sign code is a unique identifier for a sign design, and it generally has one sign description. As an example, SP-477B sign description is “BUS STOP SIGN (BUS & HANDICAP SYMBOLS) NO STANDING W/ SINGLE ARROW”. DOT does not maintain a separate guide/legend of sign codes. Excel pivot tables or other software can summarize the list of codes and their descriptions, if desired.

For most signs, all sign instances with the same sign code are physically the same. However, there are several exceptions where sign text can vary. “SPECIAL,” “INSERT” AND “RIDER” are examples of such codes. “SPECIAL” signs are often used for events, or for ceremonial street renaming, and “INSERT” AND “RIDER” are used for signs that appear on or below other signs. These generic codes have fallen out of use at DOT, but the data still contains examples.

DOT also uses generic sign codes for Bus Stop route, destination and locator panels, for some speed limit signs, and in several other cases. These sign codes have descriptions that indicate there is a variable element to the sign. An example would be the bus stop route sign, with the description “LOCAL MTA BUS ROUTE PANEL (TEXT TO BE MODIFIED AS REQUESTED)” or a speed limit sign, with the description “SPEED LIMIT XX SPEED CHECKED BY RADAR (XX = SPEED TO BE DETERMINED).”


Thank you,
-NYC Department of Transportation

Thank you for your dataset inquiry. The Parking Regulation and Signs dataset is scheduled for an update for December, 2019.

The answers to your question are as follows:
Sign sequence (SRP_Seq)- The unique identifier of the Sign Order. One sign order may contain multiples of the same sign.
Distance from the curb line (SR_Distx)- The distance between the curb and the sign in feet.
Arrow points (SR_Arrow)- If the sign contains an arrow (eg: One-Way Sign), the column describes the direction of the arrow, otherwise it is NULL.
Sign code (SR_Mutcd_Code)- The unique identifier of the sign based on the design.

tickets.question:
How can I convert columns sign_x_coord and sign_y_coord into real GPS coordinates? These columns don't appear to be true longitude or latitude coordinates. What type of numbers are they? I'm looking for decimal degree coordinates like this:

https://www.gps-coordinates.net/gps-coordinates-converter
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your inquiry. Unfortunately, the Parking Regulation and Location Sign system does not provide latitude (lat) and longitude (long) information, only X,Y. New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) maintains a website for all New York City Parking Regulation Signs mapped, please visit: https://nycdotsigns.net/.
You may also use Geographic Information System (GIS) applications such as ESRI ArcGIS or the free open-source platform QGIS to process X,Y conversions to Lat, Long, some basic application knowledge is required, see information below:

1) Using ArcGIS- license required
Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table. More information about the tool on the ArcGIS website:https://desktop.arcgis.com/en/arcmap/latest/manage-data/tables/calculating-area-length-and-other-geometric-properties.htm
ESRI community forum (https://community.esri.com/t5/arcgis-api-for-flex-questions/how-to-convert-x-y-to-lat-long/td-p/353854).

To do:
1. Load the data into the application as a CSV, add new columns in the attribute table (long and lat).
2. Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table (right click on the column header) to process the conversion. Fill in as follows:
a. Coordinates system of the data sources: NAD1983 State Plane New York Long Island FIPS 3104 Feet
b. Use coordinate system of the data frame: WGS 1984
c. Units: Decimal Degree

2) Using QGIS- free to download
More information from this blog: https://www.gisoutlook.com/2020/05/coordinate-conversion-process-in-qgis.html

To do:
Import CSV file: Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Delaminated Text Layer (CSV file)-> (keep everything else as default) only change Geometry CRS: EPSG:2263- NAD83/ New York Long Island (ftUS) -> add
Export layer+ Conversion: Export-> Save Feature As-> File Name: (select where to save the new file) Fill in as follows:
a. Format: CSV
b. CRS: EPSG:4326- WGS 84
c. Geometry: AS_XY

tickets.question:
the columns sign_x_coord and sign_y_coord are documented as longitude, latitude. However, the data provided doesn't seem to be valid. latitude ranges from -90 to 90, and longitude -180 to 180.

1006449, 219326

So how do I convert sign_x_coord and sign_y_coord to longitude, latitude values?
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your request on Parking Regulation Sign locations. The coordinate system for the signs are in X,Y, you will need to convert to Latitude and Longitude. One method is to use a Geographic Information Systems (GIS) system application like ArcMap or QGIS, note: some basic GIS knowledge required.
ArcMap-:
1. Download the data as CSV or shapefile
2. If using CSV, load the data into the application as a CSV. Or load the shapefile.
3. Right click on the layer to open an attribute table. Add two new columns in the attribute table, "Lat", "Long".
4. Use the Calculate Geometry tool in the attribute table (right click on the column header) to process the conversion. Fill in as follows:
a. Coordinates system of the data sources: NAD1983 State Plane New York Long Island FIPS 3104 Feet
b. Use coordinate system of the data frame: WGS 1984
c. Units: Decimal Degree

QGIS-: Free and Open Source
1. Import CSV file: Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Delaminated Text Layer (CSV file)-> (keep everything else as default) only change Geometry CRS: EPSG:2263- NAD83/ New York Long Island (ftUS) -> add
2. Export layer+ Conversion: Export-> Save Feature As-> File Name: (select where to save the new file) Fill in as follows:
3. a. Format: CSV
4. b. CRS: EPSG:4326- WGS 84
5. c. Layer Option- Geometry: AS_XY

Thank you,
NYC Department of Transportation

tickets.question:
Hi HPD & Open Data,
 
I hope all is well. 
 
I’m reaching out to ask some questions about the HPD Complaints data.
 
My Questions:
- In the HPD complaints data, there are about 14 million rows - however there are only about 7 million unique complaint IDs
    - Is there duplication in this data?
    - In poking around, it seems that there can be multiple problems assigned to a complaint
        - What is the column problemid used for?
        - I see that there can be multiple problems per complaint, how does this work?
            - (ie is it just that someone specifies multiple issues when they file a complaint)
 
Please clarify and thank you!!
tickets.reply:
Each row in this dataset represents a problem reported by a complainant, so each row would not be a unique complaint ID. One ‘complaint’ may be associated with one or more ‘problems.’ Problems are closed if a tenant verifies that the condition was corrected or an inspection result is entered by an HPD inspector. A complaint is closed when all associated problems are closed.
 
For example:
- Complaint ID 10337632 has two Problem IDs attached: 21016592 and 21016593
- 21016592 is related to no heat in the apartment, which is categorized as emergency 
- 21016593 is related to a broken appliance in the kitchen, which is categorized as non-emergency.
 
As you can see, this complaint has multiple problems (or distinct issues) that the agency has a varying ways to respond to. 
 
I hope this helps and please reach out to [email] if you have any additional questions. 
 
Best,
HPD Open Data Team

Could you please share how your team measures or calculates the number of public restrooms? Any information about your methodology or data sources would be greatly appreciated. 
Thank you for time and assistance.

Several issues in the Directory of Playgrounds feed (DPR_Playgrounds_001.json), found while building a free NYC public playground map:
1. Two records have latitude and longitude transposed. Grady Playground (B275) and Governor Smith Playground (X210) both map into the Indian Ocean.
2. Grady Playground's Prop_ID is "D", which appears malformed. Its Playground_ID (B275) is correct.
3. The ADA_Accessible_Comfort_Station field has four values for three states. "Not Accessible" and "NotAccessible" appear as separate values.
4. The feed regenerates daily, so its Last-Modified header always shows the current date. I could not determine when the content was last substantively revised, which makes it difficult to tell users how current the accessibility information is.
5. Comparing this feed against the Public Restrooms dataset (i7jb-7jku), the two sources disagree on restroom accessibility for 231 playgrounds.
6. Three playgrounds have facility pages on nycgovparks.org that are not reachable through the usual navigation: Grady (197), Tilyou (285), and Governor Smith (971).
The map is at playdar.netlify.app if useful. It's free and has no ads. Happy to share full reconciliation notes.
tickets.reply:
Apologies for the delayed response.
The Directory of Playgrounds JSON feed was inaccurate and has been archived. This dataset has been replaced by Playgrounds with Dedicated Children's Areas (DCAs) (j55h-3upk on Open Data) and here is the mapped data (asdj-rj9b on Open Data). Regarding the specific errors you mentioned: 

1. Two records have latitude and longitude transposed. Grady Playground (B275) and Governor Smith Playground (X210) both map into the Indian Ocean.
--> Grady's location has been corrected. Governor Smith Playground is now under the jurisdiction of the Dept of Education (DOE) so no longer appears in this data. 

2. Grady Playground's Prop_ID is "D", which appears malformed. Its Playground_ID (B275) is correct.
--> Fixed. 

3. The ADA_Accessible_Comfort_Station field has four values for three states. "Not Accessible" and "NotAccessible" appear as separate values.
--> Accessibility information is on the Parks website and is scheduled to be added to this dataset in the near future. 

4. The feed regenerates daily, so its Last-Modified header always shows the current date. I could not determine when the content was last substantively revised, which makes it difficult to tell users how current the accessibility information is.
--> This field does not appear in the new dataset.

5. Comparing this feed against the Public Restrooms dataset (i7jb-7jku), the two sources disagree on restroom accessibility for 231 playgrounds.
--> Accessibility information is on the Parks website and we're working on adding it to Open Data in the future.

6. Three playgrounds have facility pages on nycgovparks.org that are not reachable through the usual navigation: Grady (197), Tilyou (285), and Governor Smith (971).
--> Grady Playground's webpage navigation has been corrected. Tilyou is no longer a Parks property and has been removed from the website. Gov Smith is no longer a Parks property and is in the process of being removed from the website. 

Thanks for your inquiry and attention to detail!

tickets.question:

I'm developing ***, an independent restroom-finding application that aims to help people locate bathrooms and contribute firsthand information about them.

tickets.reply: Per the Open Data Law (https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/open-data-law/), users do not need a license in order to copy, reuse, or share the data on NYC Open Data. New York City's open data is free for anyone to use for any purpose they see fit. We do not require, but encourage users to cite the data and share the results under a similarly permissive license. Our team would love to see the results of your analysis! Once they're done, please submit any project that uses NYC Open Data to be featured on our Project Gallery (https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/projects/) via this submission form: https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/project-submit/.

tickets.question:

For context, I've been cross-referencing against the NYC Planning "LION 23C" street-network archive (nyclion_23c.zip) as a proxy, and it resolves most but not all of the PhysicalID mismatches I'm seeing -- I'd like to confirm whether that's actually the right reference or a coincidentally similar one.

tickets.reply:
First, regarding zip codes that spread outside of NYC. Are you using the zip codes as a list, or is this a mapping error? Because zip codes that spread outside the city ARE included if they have any overlap inside the five boroughs. What was excluded was from the mapping component which "trimmed" the boundaries of those zip codes to what just is within the city boundaries. If you are creating a map and that is where you're seeing the error it would be helpful to know which values aren't trimmed correctly. 

Second, about the single building zip codes, do you happen to have a list of the ones you found? Or if you have the modified version of the dataset you are using I can do a comparison. We are looking into this, but having a list would expedite the work!

tickets.question:
Edit:
Why does this dataset differ from the Storefronts Reported Vacant or Not (Filing Year 2020 - 2021) and Storefronts Reported Vacant or Not (Filing Year 2019 - 2020) datasets? When you sum the total number of Class one, two, and four properties in each filing year from the aggregated datasets (Class One dataset and class two and four dataset) and from the non-aggregated datasets (Storefronts reported vacant or not) the totals do not match. For 2019, I get 70,202 class one, two, and four properties from the aggregated dataset and 75,250 from the non-aggregated dataset. Similarly, for 2020, I get 72,325 vs. 75,540. Any help answering why the numbers differ would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks!
*****
--------------------------
Original:
From what dataset is this data aggregated? Is it the Storefronts Reported Vacant or Not dataset?

Thanks!
*****
tickets.reply:
Statistical reporting uses only the main registrations filed for each calendar year. Due to the variations in data collected, class one statistics are reported separately from Classes 2 and 4 statistics for each calendar year.

For Storefronts Reported Vacant or Not, the main registration filings are the primary source of information for parcel-level status, with supplemental registry updates providing additional information for Classes 2 and 4. Some owners who did not file main registrations or who filed main registrations with missing information provided information on both the 12/31 and 6/30 vacancy status of storefronts in their properties in the supplemental filing. For Class 1, only the main registration is used as the source of information for parcel-level status. By law, most class 1 properties (i.e., properties with leased class 1 storefronts) are not required to register during the calendar year. Properties that are required to register are not required to provide supplemental information.




Thank you,
- NYC DOF

tickets.question:
"DSNY Districts With Disposal Vendor Assignments" is overwritten upon each update. The information in it, which explains where refuse, recycling and organics are discharged for each of NYC's 59 community districts, is therefore relevant the present time only. However, over time District Disposal Vendor Assignments change. Historical information is lost upon each update.

Historical information on Disposal Vendor Assignments is of relevance to public information, especially in conjunction with new datasets that track where refuse is exported to over time, going back to 2018. Currently several independent dashboards are drawing from "DSNY Districts With Disposal Vendor Assignments" datasets; these dashboards work with historical as well as present flows data from other DSNY Open Datasets that do have a date column and reflect historical information.

I request either that:

1. Open data work with DSNY to amend the current reporting structure to include "data as of" or "last date updated" field. Current and past records would be in this dataset, distinguished by this date field. For users interested in current data only, it will be easy to filter by this column.

example: add a column called "DATA AS OF:" before existing columns including DISTRICT DISTRICTCODE MGP_CURB_PRI MGP_CURB_SEC MGP_EZP_PRI, etc.

this would be the easiest and most straightforward means of addressing the issue I have raised. 

OR

2. Open Data work with DSNY to create a second historical dataset going back to 2018, or the inception of this dataset, whichever is earlier, in which versions have a "data as of" field. This historical dataset would need to be updated each time the current dataset it updated.

OR

3. Open Data post historical/archived versions of this dataset going back to its inception on Open Data. I would assume that Open Data saves past submissions from DSNY for this dataset (based on my experience working for City agencies with Open Datasets prior to my retirement in 2022). Historical datasets would need to be updated each time the current dataset it updated.

Thank you for your time, 
Respectfully submitted,
*****
tickets.reply: The DSNY Districts With Disposal Vendor Assignments dataset is manually updated on an as-needed basis and is intended to show current disposal vendors used by each district and has 59 rows and 32 columns. Given pressing technological and operational demands and projects, DSNY does not currently have the staff nor resources to either add a new “last date updated” column to this dataset or create a new historical dataset given the manual nature of the data and the analysis required to determine when a change was made to any of the vendors listed going back to 2018.

tickets.question:
Hi! I have a few questions about how to find newly filed building permits in NYC.

It's my understanding that DOB NOW Build is the best place to find the latest and most up-to-date information on DOB permitting. Is it still worth querying BIS datasets like DOB Job Application Filings (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/DOB-Job-Application-Filings/ic3t-wcy2/about_data) if I am only looking for the most recently filed data? 

More specifically, my use case is to find buildings in Brooklyn that are planning new commercial and retail space. My current approach is to search DOB NOW Build Job App Filings for:
- job type = new building
- borough = brooklyn
- general_construction_work_type_ = Yes

I also filter for total_construction_floor_area > 20000 because I'm looking for larger buildings.

This works well to get a new dataset, but the info there doesn't tell me anything about commercial/retail space, as far as I can tell. So next I am attempting to get this data from PLUTO (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Primary-Land-Use-Tax-Lot-Output-PLUTO-/64uk-42ks/about_data). However, it occurs to me that PLUTO may be referring to *existing* buildings on the specified lot, rather than the *new* buildings being planned by the new building permit. tickets.reply:
From DCP: Yes, PLUTO data is about existing uses, not planned. We source our data from DOF.
From DOB: The correct data sets to reference are primarily DOB NOW: Build - Approved Permits and DOB NOW: Build - Job Application Filings. In some cases, there can be permits requested and issued in BIS on new building applications that were filed in BIS, however that set is small and will continue to decline.

tickets.question: I have a question about what is identified as "Land Use Category" 04 ("Mixed Residential & Commercial Buildings") in the data set. Please get back to me at your earliest convenience. Thank you.
tickets.reply:
Thank you for your inquiry into Department of City Planning (DCP) data. Most questions related to PLUTO/MapPLUTO can be answered by consulting the PLUTO Data Dictionary. For Land Use questions you can consult the Land Use field description and Appendix D.
 
Land Use Description: A code for the tax lot's land use category. The Department of City Planning has created 11 land use categories and assigns each BUILDING CLASS to the most appropriate land use category.   Appendix D - Land Use Categories details the relationship of building classes to land use categories.
 
Appendix D: 04-Mixed Residential and Commercial Buildings includes the following building class codes C7,D6,D7,K4,O8,R8,R9,RM,RR,RX,RZ,S* 
- *Denotes all building class classifications within that grouping
- Check Appendix C for specific DOF building class titles

In the data dictionary, there are several Tax Class columns:

PYTAXCLASS - Values as of the Final Roll for the Previous Tax Year
TENTAXCLASS - Values as of the publishing of the Tentative Assessment Roll in January
CBNTAXCLASS - Values as of the Change By Notice period in May
FINTAXCLASS - Values as of the publishing of the Final Assessment Roll in May

Hello NYC Open Data Team,
I am developing a case study using the GreenThumb data sets. I have a few questions regarding a deeper understanding of what some of the variables in the Site Visits data mean. Specifically,  a better understanding of a site's water resources based on the variables provided, without needing to dive into other data sets. I do have the Data Dictionary but I'm not confident in the Description to make assumptions. To clarify, I am not looking for quantity of water usage, merely a deeper understanding of how garden sites have access to water.

Does OnSiteService mean the site has city water service paid by the community garden? Or provided as a city support initiative to give free access to water for the garden site from the city? The majority of sites in this data set do not indicate a TRUE response for OnSiteService, yet a community garden likely needs access to water. I'd expect to see a majority of sites having OnSiteService. Aside, from RainHarvesting how else might a garden site have access to water for the plants? 

Also, are the two variables, HydrantW_in15ft and HydrantOnGardenSide, present for the purpose of NYCFD accessibility in the event of a fire? Or does it imply that the site has access (a connection) to the hydrant for use in the community garden?

Thank you for any insights you can provide to help me better understand those three variables. And many more thanks for the vast amount of meaningful and clean data that you provide.
tickets.reply:
Hello *****,
We received your inquiry from the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. Our response is as follows:

Through our inter-agency partnership with the NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), all registered GreenThumb community gardens, regardless of jurisdiction, can obtain a free hydrant permit from to access water for free from a nearby fire hydrant to irrigate their plants. More details are available in the Hydrant Access section of The Greenthumb Gardeners’ Handbook, which can be found in multiple languages here: The GreenThumb Gardeners’ Handbook : NYC Parks For an informational video on the mechanics of accessing the hydrant, GreenThumb has provided a YouTube video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uIvTTO3IFL0&pp=ygUSaHlkcmFudCBncmVlbnRodW1i – and more details are available in The GreenThumb Gardeners’ Handbook.
 
Hydrant distance from the garden gate may vary. More details on hydrant locations and for mapping distances to garden centroids or polygons can be found in this dataset: NYCDEP Citywide Hydrants | NYC Open Data Both the HydrantW_in15ft and HydrantOnGardenSide variables are indicative of hydrant placement relative to the garden gate. GreenThumb does provide garden hoses for registered groups during our spring supply distributions, but gardens reliant on hydrants across the street may face additional challenges with traffic damaging hoses despite the use of hose protectors.
 
OnSiteService is indicative of a garden that has an internal water system that has been installed by NYC Parks with funding from an elected official for this capital project. More details on this process can be found on page 38 of The GreenThumb Gardeners’ Handbook as well as by watching Building the Garden: Advocating for Discretionary Funding.

Best,
Department of Parks and Recreation (PARKS)

tickets.question: Please explain the existing public sources used to generate this dataset on a monthly basis, and the detailed process used to generte the monthly file from those sources (including relevant business logic).
tickets.reply:
The Monthly Rolling Sales file is created by using sales data from ACRIS. This monthly rolling sales file contains 12-months of property sales within New York City, excluding “DELETED” and “Utility” Property Sales. The 12-month timeframe is dynamic and contains the previous 12 months of sales before the reporting month. For instance, for the reporting month of September 2025, we would have the rolling sales reports with sale dates from September 2024 to August 2025.
 
The ACRIS datasets can be found in the Open Data Portal by searching on the keyword “ACRIS”. The building class of a property is from the ACRIS datasets at the time of sale and the tax class values are based on the building class values.

I have a question regarding the APPENDIX D – A table of Restrictive Declarations indicating requirements applicable to identified tax lots associated with an adopted zoning map amendment, that I hope you can answer for me.

What is the difference between the pdf file:

https://zr.planning.nyc.gov/sites/default/files/appendix/21241/APPENDIX%20D%20%E2%80%94%20Zoning%20Map%20Amendment%20%28%22D%22%29%20Restrictive%20Declarations.pdf

Thank you
tickets.reply:
Thank you for contacting the NYC Open Data Helpdesk! We appreciate your patience as we worked on this response. A restrictive declaration (RD) is a covenant recorded against a specific property that places conditions on a property’s future use and development.
- Parks RD GIS Layer https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Recreation/Restrictive-Declaration-Sites/cmni-fvnx/about_data
    - This is a Parks general layer that shows built privately maintained sites that are subject a Parks M&O agreements which is usually an attachment to a RD. Most were triggered by zoning actions such as waterfront certification and large-scale development and the M&O codifies the developer’s obligation to build and maintain the open space.
- https://zr.planning.nyc.gov/sites/default/files/appendix/21241/APPENDIX%20D%20%E2%80%94%20Zoning%20Map%20Amendment%20%28%22D%22%29%20Restrictive%20Declarations.pdf
    - These sites are subject to RD which indicates specific requirements related to adopted zoning map amendment. The requirements are not necessarily related open space. For example, RD # D-37 (Block 13957 Lot 12) requires the property owner to maintain a brick wall along the parcel’s 92nd St boundary. Not relevant for tracking RDs with a park obligations.    
 
There is no standalone list of RD sites not maintained by Parks.

Thank you,
NYC Department of Parks and Recreation (PARKS)

tickets.question:
1. Does the dataset cover all parks within NYC, regardless of their management/ownership—whether federal, state, city, or non-profit organizations? Or is it limited to parks under the city's ownership or management?

2. Does the "acquisition date" indicate the date the park property was officially acquired by the city government?

3. Is there a distinction between the "acquisition date" and the year a park was established? If so, could you elucidate the difference?
tickets.reply:
Please see the responses to your questions below. If you have any follow up questions, you can reach out to *****.
 
1. Acquisition date refers to the date it came under NYC Park’s jurisdiction/management. When it is private property acquired for a park purpose, the acquisition date and the title vesting date is the same. We acquire property that is often already city-owned, and perhaps used initially for a different purpose, in that case the acquisition date still only reflects the date our agency took control of the parcel.
2. Jurisdiction refers to management, it may have nothing to do with the land acquisition process. For instance, land for jointly-operated playgrounds was usually acquired for school and park purposes. The land acquisition process was approved by the other government bodies, typically the Board of Estimate (BOE) up until the early 1980s, after consulting with NYC Parks. Upon the BOE’s approval, the City’s Law Department would acquire the property through whatever legal channels necessary, and upon vesting title, the land came under the control of the Department of Education and NYC Parks to execute the purpose for which the parcel was acquired. In other instances, NYC Parks may directly seek out a parcel of land for a park-related purpose and lobby for its acquisition with elected officials, community stakeholders, and seek official city authorization to acquire through the acquisition process outlined on our website, ULURP.
3. If a parcel is acquired through a negotiated purchase with a private entity, a council member may choose to allocate funding towards that acquisition. If funding has already been secured by other means, the Council’s role in the ULURP process is to either vote on the action or allow it to pass by taking no action. The roles of the Council, the City Planning Commission, the community board, the borough president, and mayor’s in the ULURP process are outline on City Planning’s website here: https://www.nyc.gov/site/planning/applicants/applicant-portal/step5-ulurp-process.page
 
Thanks,
NYC Parks Open Data Team

tickets.question:
Hello NYC Parks / NYC Open Data team,

Following my messages of October 8 and 9 (tickets #13107 and #13111), I have five more questions, about Forestry Planting Spaces (82zj-84is), Forestry Tree Points (hn5i-inap) and Forestry Risk Assessments (259a-b6s7).

1. Duplicate planting spaces. Planting Spaces (82zj-84is) has 1,091,709 rows but only 1,084,845 distinct GlobalIDs: 6,864 GlobalIDs appear exactly twice, and each pair is identical on all 35 columns, OBJECTID included (for example GlobalID 00007383-6466-4C33-A715-3523186EEF66, OBJECTID 11041439). This follows question 3 of my message of October 9 on row identifiers. Is the duplication an artefact of the export, and will the copies be removed at the next refresh?
2. Implausible diameters. In Tree Points (hn5i-inap), 17 standing trees (TPStructure Full) have a DBH over 120 inches. Two examples: OBJECTID 1268531 (northern red oak, Quercus rubra) at 2,427 inches, and OBJECTID 2412695 (Chinese elm, Ulmus parvifolia) at 1,310 inches. Could you confirm or correct these values? Is there an accepted maximum, or a validation rule, for DBH in ForMS?
3. DBH of 0 and blank DBH. In Tree Points, DBH is 0 on 22,549 rows (644 of them standing trees, TPStructure Full) and blank on 24,840 rows (76 of them standing trees). Does 0 mean "not measured" or "not applicable", or is it a real measurement (for example a newly planted tree below measuring height)? Do 0 and blank mean different things? This is separate from my question 2 of October 9 about Retired and Stump rows.
4. Risk assessments on Sidewalk Rating inspections. The Risk Assessments (259a-b6s7) description says risk assessments are sub-components of inspections where Type = Level 2, but some are attached to "Sidewalk Rating" inspections. Two examples: objectid 184915 (inspection D3F9B780-63F8-4CFB-BD8F-F559180C4B9E, created 2018-03-06, "No Visible Defect", rating 3) and objectid 3477976 (inspection F152DC53-0B44-45D5-BFBB-C0F2D8561511, created 2021-03-10, "Root Problems", rating 3). Are risk assessments routinely scored during sidewalk inspections, and since when? Does Tree Points RiskRating take the most recent assessment from any inspection type, so that a sidewalk inspection's rating of 3 can replace an earlier Level 2 rating of 6 or 7, as on tree points 2496399 and 202797? If so, could the description be updated?
5. "DNP" in planting space status. In Planting Spaces (82zj-84is), PSStatus has the values "Empty - DNP" (1,690 spaces) and "Retired - DNP" (1,442 spaces), counted over distinct spaces. What does DNP stand for? Should an "Empty - DNP" space be counted as available planting capacity? The data dictionary entry for PSStatus (row 2.021) says only "Indicates if planting space is populated, empty, or retired"; could the values be listed with definitions?
Thank you,
***
tickets.reply:
Hi ****,
Thanks for all of your questions about the ForMS (Forestry) datasets. I’ve included responses to all three of your inquiries (13107, 13111, 13120) in this email, and I’ve updated the data dictionary where possible, so feel free to take another look. Please see below and reach out if you need clarity on anything else.

1. re: Duplicate planting spaces. Duplicates that appeared in error were removed by the 10/21 data refresh.
2. re: Implausible diameters. These values are attributed to manual data entry errors. There is no validation rule for DBH values in ForMS. While these trees can be put into a queue for re-inspection, we have no timeline as to when the values will be updated to correct the errors.
3. re: DBH of 0 and blank DBH. Generally speaking, zeros and blanks in the DBH field are likely for trees that originated as stumps, and had no DBH to measure. DBH is required field for Tree Points, but blanks and zeros are not part of the data validation for that field. These values for the standing trees are likely due to data entry errors. There is no validation rule for DBH values in ForMS.
4. re: Risk assessments on Sidewalk Rating inspections. Yes, Risk Assessments are a part of Sidewalk inspections, and the tree point takes the most recent risk rating from any inspection type that has a risk assessment (Level 2, Level 3, and Sidewalk Rating Inspection).
5. “DNP” in planting space status. DNP stands for “Do Not Plant” and is a designation used by a Forester to indicate this particular planting space is no longer viable for various reasons (utilities, underground vaults, etc.)

Hi NYC Open Data,
I've been working with this dataset and observed that most of the sections of piers or reclaimed land in the East River off the west coastline of Brooklyn are labeled as being a part of the Manhattan borough. The sections are south of the Brooklyn Bridge, and west of Brooklyn Heights and the Columbia Waterfront. There are also a few docks or piers west of Williamsburg.

I've searched online to try to find more information about this and haven't found anything.

I assume these may be labeled in this way because of a policy or agreement that defines everything west of the Brooklyn coastline (all area of the East River) is part of Manhattan, and these sections fall within those boundaries or requirements.

Interestingly, most of Brooklyn Bridge Park is considered part of Manhattan, but other developed waterfront areas like John Street Park are not.

I'm curious to know more about the history of this if it is not an error, or of documents where these rules are defined. Do you know why these sections that are physically connected with Brooklyn are labeled as part of Manhattan?
tickets.reply:
This is not an error, the Borough Boundaries extend into the waterways and are defined in the City Charter (https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/newyorkcity/latest/NYCadmin/0-0-0-94).  The Manhattan boundary extends to the "low-water mark on the shore of Long Island" so you will also notice this for any piers in Queens along the East River.

The borough of Manhattan shall consist of the territory known as New York county... thence across the East river to the low-water mark on the shore of Long Island, so as to include Randall's Island and Ward's Island; thence along the low-water mark on the shore of Long Island to the southerly side of Red Hook; thence across the Upper bay to the westerly boundary of the state...

Thank you,
-DCP Open Data Team

I understand that currently in DOBNow, the C of O type (Final vs. Temporary) is only viewable within the attached PDF. However, is there any way to infer or access this information via the DOBNow OpenData dataset?

On a different note, Also, is filing_status_raw the same as or related to c_of_o_filing_type, or are they entirely different?

tickets.reply: For DOB NOW, the following are all considered "temporary" and not "final": initial, renewal with change, renewal without change.

tickets.question:
Dear NYC Open Data team and Department of Health and Mental Hygiene,

I'm building *** a free public website, still in development, that helps families read child care inspection records in plain language. Each provider's page shows what the city or state published (inspections, the rules cited, corrections), with the date and a link back to the official record.

New York City publishes its child care programs and their inspections in NYC Child Care Connect (a816-healthpsi.nyc.gov), and on NYC Open Data: the dataset gy3q-4tzp, licensed Public Domain and updated daily, lists 2,748 programs with their ages, capacity and location, including the day care centers the State's own dataset leaves out, while the open inspections dataset (dsg6-ifza) is no longer updated. NYC.gov's terms say "All rights are reserved" and send permission requests to the agency, so we have collected and shown nothing from New York City, and won't until we hear from you. Until then we also leave out the State's own records of programs in the five boroughs.

Could you tell me three things? First, whether we may publish the city's programs from the Public Domain dataset gy3q-4tzp alone, and nothing from Child Care Connect, unless DOHMH prefers otherwise; NYC Open Data's FAQ says "There are no restrictions on the use of Open Data". Second, whether DOHMH would resume updating the open child care inspections dataset (dsg6-ifza), or permit a once-a-day read of NYC Child Care Connect, at a gentle pace (one request a second at most, or slower if you prefer, with a User-Agent that names the project and gives its web address). Third, whether you'd like us to credit the records in a particular way.

How we'd use them: they would be free to read for everyone, with no account needed, and we never sell or license New York City's records. We name no people: organizations only, never staff, owners who are individuals, or home-based providers by their own name, and a home-based provider is shown by its city and ZIP code only. Every finding shows its date and links to your record, and anyone who believes a record is wrong is sent to your correction process. We may offer paid services built on other data (for example, federal nursing-home data), and optional conveniences such as change alerts, but New York City's records themselves stay free.

If automated reading isn't something you allow, I'll respect that. We'll show a note that New York City's records are on your site, with a link, rather than collecting them.

Thank you for your time.

***
